articles.title: Kemi Badenoch wants Reform voters to 'come back'
articles.summary: Kemi Badenoch wants Reform voters to 'come back'
articles.body:
Kemi Badenoch has said she would rather have another general election than do a deal with Reform UK if no party wins the next election.

In an interview with the BBC's Chris Mason the Tory party leader said she said that Nigel Farage's Reform Party are "neck deep in scandal" and joining forces with them would "just be one problem after another", adding I don't have time for that.

The Conservative Party are meeting in Birmingham for their annual conference.

articles.title: Is there a MAGA after Trump?
articles.summary: From the Epstein files to the war on Iran, Josh Rushing examines the cracks forming within MAGA in Trump’s second term.
articles.body:
Donald Trump still decides who gets to call themselves MAGA – but what happens when that power has to pass to someone else?

Josh Rushing is joined by Rina Shah, a Republican strategist and one of the original Never Trumpers, and Emma Doyle, former deputy chief of staff in Trump’s first administration, to ask whether MAGA can outgrow its frontman, or whether, as both guests agree, MAGA simply is Donald Trump.

articles.title: Irã convoca embaixador da França após confrontos com estudantes | G1
articles.standfirst: Governo iraniano acusou autoridades francesas de violência e de violações de direitos humanos durante protestos por melhores condições nas escolas.
articles.summary: Governo iraniano acusou autoridades francesas de violência e de violações de direitos humanos durante protestos por melhores condições nas escolas.
articles.body:
O Irã convocou o embaixador da França em Teerã, Pierre Cochard , para questionar a violência usada pelas autoridades francesas contra os manifestantes que reivindicam melhores condições nas escolas de ensino médio . A convocação ocorreu nesta terça-feira (6), após vários dias de confrontos entre policiais e estudantes durante os protestos, segundo a imprensa estatal iraniana.

O governo do Irã acusou a França de adotar um "tratamento violento" contra os manifestantes e de cometer "violações graves e flagrantes dos direitos humanos" durante os atos, que começaram no fim do mês passado e foram marcados por episódios de violência.

As relações entre França e Irã vêm se deteriorando há meses. Em agosto, os dois países expulsaram diplomatas um do outro.

O Irã também registrou uma onda de protestos contra o governo em janeiro . Na época, as autoridades disseram que mais de 3.000 pessoas morreram e atribuíram a violência a "atos terroristas" orquestrados pelos Estados Unidos e por Israel .

Organizações não governamentais sediadas no exterior, porém, afirmam que as forças de segurança iranianas abriram fogo contra os manifestantes.

Os protestos antigovernamentais que se espalharam pelo Irã, no começo deste ano, foram reprimidos na maior operação do tipo da história recente da República Islâmica.

Especialistas da Organização das Nações Unidas afirmaram que pelo menos 24 pessoas foram executadas por crimes relacionados aos protestos de janeiro. Já a Human Rights Watch afirmou que cerca de 50 outras pessoas foram executadas por acusações vagas relacionadas à segurança nacional.

articles.summary: British adventurer back in UK after 28-year trek on foot around the world
articles.body:
British adventurer back in UK after 28-year trek on foot around the world

After 28 years and a 50,000km round-the-world trek on foot, Karl Bushby is back on British soil. Bushby set out from Punta Arenas, Chile, in November 1988, aiming to get to Hull in the UK under his own power. After swimming the English Channel, he has one last leg to go.

articles.title: Birzeit University memorial destruction aims to crush Palestinian memory
articles.summary: Israeli soldiers removed the monument to students and alumni killed by Israel and replaced it with a fig sapling.
articles.body:
After Israeli soldiers stormed Birzeit University near Ramallah to demolish a stone memorial dedicated to dead students, Rania Washaha, 47, felt the pain of bereavement again.

Her brother, Fadi, 34, was shot in the head by an Israeli soldier near the northern entrance to el-Bireh in the central West Bank in May 2021.

His name was among the 38 students from the university killed by Israel and listed on the stone pillar known as the Martyrs’ Monument.

Israeli soldiers raided the university campus at dawn on Monday, accompanied by 10 military vehicles. A bulldozer demolished the pillar, and soldiers took away the marble stone. In its place, the Israelis left a planter containing a fig sapling, bearing the inscription: “Water it twice.”

This raid marks the fifth Israeli incursion into the campus since the beginning of 2026 and the 28th since 2002.

Birzeit University’s administration condemned the recent raid, describing the destruction of the Martyrs’ Monument as a violation of international law and an attack on education and national memory.

“Bulldozers won’t erase the memory of the martyrs, military vehicles won’t extinguish the light of knowledge, and these assaults won’t break the university’s resolve to pursue its academic and national mission,” a statement by the university pledged.

It came 10 days after another incursion by Israeli forces during the daytime, a day before the start of the new fall semester.

Nardeen al-Memi, the university’s public relations and media officer, told Al Jazeera in the brief minutes of their incursion, Israeli soldiers approached the monument for the first time and photographed it.

The Martyrs’ Monument was erected between 1994 and 1996, bearing the names of students and alumni at Birzeit killed by Israeli forces. The list starts with Sharaf al-Tayyibi, who was shot dead by Israeli forces on the campus in 1984. The names of other students and alumni were added during the years that followed.

“The last name inscribed on the monument was that of student Omar al-Naasan, whom soldiers killed in al-Mughayyir east of Ramallah on September 2 while he was confronting settler incursions,” said Nardeen. “Days after his death, his father came and personally wrote his son’s name on the monument.”

University students organised a protest at the site of the destroyed memorial on Tuesday afternoon, most viewing it as an Israeli attempt to intimidate them.

Sami Adel, a Birzeit student who wanted to use a pseudonym due to his fear of being detained, told Al Jazeera the memorial holds a place in the heart of everyone who has attended the university since the 1990s.

In recent years, Israel has tried to suppress any student activity dedicated to commemorating the martyrs, he said.

“Soldiers detained me for several hours three weeks ago and threatened that if I participated in any political student activity on campus, I would face a long and harsh detention,” he added.

The removal of the memorial is part of a broader Israeli policy targeting memorials dedicated to Palestinians killed by Israel in the occupied West Bank.

The Israeli far-right has made the issue part of its campaign to erase markers of Palestinian identity.

Zvi Sukkot, a member of the Knesset from the Religious Zionism Party, destroyed one such memorial in the village of Madama, south of Nablus, with a sledgehammer in August. The Israeli military later said that it routinely removes “symbols of incitement”.

Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich submitted a list of approximately 40 Palestinian memorials, proposing their destruction, to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

There has been a wider targeting of civic and cultural symbols across the West Bank, particularly in Jenin, by Israeli authorities.

“Jenin Horse”, a monument constructed from the wreckage left behind by an Israeli incursion into the city, was removed. A memorial dedicated to Al Jazeera journalist Shireen Abu Akleh in Jenin was also targeted in 2023.

A cemetery containing the bodies of Iraqi soldiers killed during the 1948 war, also located in Jenin, has been raided by Israelis from illegal settlements.

Other landmarks embedded in the city’s collective memory, including the “Watermelon Roundabout”, have also been targeted.

Israel’s targeting of Palestine’s collective memory has coincided with a wider campaign of suppression in the occupied West Bank.

Palestinian universities have been a particular target in this pressure campaign, with campuses raided, students detained, and strict restrictions on activities and events within university grounds.

Israeli authorities are likely focusing on Palestinian universities because they hold a special significance for Palestinian resistance. They historically served as spaces for anti-occupation activism and have been an integral part of the Palestinian political landscape for decades.

Political analyst Mohammed al-Qeeq, who served as president of the Birzeit University Student Council between 2006 and 2007, told Al Jazeera that Israel has targeted writers, influencers, and activists, along with students, to deter any resistance to the occupation.

Universities have historically served as a “fundamental pillar” of Palestinian resilience and identity.

“Israel had also sought to weaken Palestinian political and social cohesion inside universities by deepening divisions between factions and creating chaos”, he said.

For Rania, the memorial served to cement the names of the martyred students in the minds of the next generation of Berzeit students, including her brother’s.

“I cannot deny that I felt a pang of anguish when the memorial was demolished,” she told Al Jazeera. “I realised the goal wasn’t simply to uproot a physical object; I felt the suppressed violence Israel inflicts upon us.”

The memorial, constructed in 1996, stood on the campus when Fadi studied at Birzeit University. He had been arrested multiple times, spending a total of eight years in detention, and Israel denied Fadi the chance to wear a graduation gown.

“He didn’t even complete two years of study due to repeated arrests and injuries from soldiers’ gunfire,” Rania said. “Yet, he loved Birzeit University dearly and would stand by the memorial, contemplating the names of the student martyrs, never knowing that his own name would one day be added to theirs.”

This year, Rania’s son enrolled at Birzeit University as a first-year student. Shortly before classes started last September, an Israeli officer phoned him, threatening him if he participated in any student activities on campus. “Remember what we did to your uncle,” they warned him.

articles.title: UK special forces could face prosecution as Afghanistan evidence referred to police
articles.summary: Evidence relating to a number of detention operations carried out by British personnel between 2010 and 2013 is being examined.
articles.body:
UK special forces (UKSF) personnel could face prosecution after evidence found following enquiries by the SAS Inquiry, suggesting serious offences may have been committed in Afghanistan, was handed to the military police.

The evidence came to light in court proceedings on Monday and is the first time the inquiry has publicly acknowledged that its findings could lead to criminal prosecutions.

The referral - made by UKSF earlier this year - was required under the Armed Forces Act, which defines Schedule 2 serious offences as including murder and manslaughter.

It relates to a number of detention operations carried out by British personnel between 2010 and 2013.

The Ministry of Defence (MoD) found the evidence earlier this year, following investigation by the SAS Inquiry, and then UKSF referred it to the military police's Defence Serious Crime Unit (DSCU), a specialist unit set up in 2022 to deal with the most serious crimes.

Court documents obtained by the BBC suggest that the DSCU has undertaken a scoping exercise of the evidence, but the unit has paused any criminal investigations until the inquiry has been concluded.

Separately, the MoD told the BBC it was deemed inappropriate for criminal investigations to be undertaken while the inquiry was still ongoing.

The Independent Inquiry relating to Afghanistan is examining allegations that the British Army's Special Air Service (SAS) unlawfully killed people during detention operations in Afghanistan between 2010 and 2013, and that senior officials sought to cover up the true circumstances of the killings.

BBC Panorama has been investigating allegations the SAS executed handcuffed civilians and children, for more than eight years. The public inquiry was established in 2022 in the wake of Panorama's revelations.

The DSCU referral came to light during a High Court hearing brought by a witness to the inquiry.

The witness, a senior British military officer who served in Afghanistan, has won permission to have the inquiry judicially reviewed after military witnesses' legal teams were excluded from closed-door evidence hearings with whistleblowers.

Much of the public inquiry's evidence is being heard in secret.

Lawyers for the senior officer argued the process was unfair and the officer should have an opportunity to question the whistleblowers, either in person or through his lawyers, regarding any allegations made against him.

The inquiry's lawyers said it "must be able to obtain highly sensitive information" from people who may be concerned about giving evidence.

They said protected witnesses had raised fears of "grievous consequences by UKSF" if their identities were revealed.

articles.title: Mom dead, baby critically injured after being pushed from Bronx balcony; police seek ex-boyfriend
articles.summary: A 23-year-old woman and a baby fell from a Bronx apartment in New York City on Tuesday, a fall that left the woman dead and the baby in critical condition.
articles.body: A 23-year-old woman and her baby were pushed from an apartment balcony in New York City on Tuesday, leaving the woman dead and the baby in critical condition, police sources told NBC News. A spokesperson for the NYPD said the incident happened in the early hours of Tuesday morning at 2550 Olinville Avenue in the Bronx. The spokesperson said that upon arrival, the woman and baby had “injuries indicative of falling from an elevated position.” The mother, who police did not identify, and her baby were transported to a nearby hospital. The 23-year-old died from her injuries while her baby — who is under 1-year-old and a girl, according to police sources — remains in critical condition. There are no arrests at this time, according to the spokesperson, and the investigation remains ongoing. Police sources say that the mother was holding the baby when they were pushed off of the balcony. NBC New York reports that police are reviewing video of a person wearing a hoodie leaving the vicinity shortly after the crime occurred. The person seen leaving the area is believed to be the person who pushed the pair, according to police sources. However, NYPD detectives are looking to question the ex-boyfriend of the 23-year-old-woman, according to police sources. The sources did not name the man they are looking for. They have not linked the ex-boyfriend to the person who left the area wearing a hoodie. Witnesses reported hearing a disturbance in the woman’s apartment before she fell to her death, according to the sources. Police sources said there is a history of domestic violence at the woman’s address. It is unclear how high the woman and the baby were before they plunged to the ground below.

articles.title: What is pneumonic plague and how does it spread?
articles.summary: The death of a worker from a Russian lab that researches plague has prompted questions about the disease.
articles.body:
The World Health Organization has asked Russia for more information on the death of a worker at a Siberian plague research laboratory.

It is still not clear exactly what led to the worker falling ill, but media reports have led to a flurry of speculation.

Russian officials are still investigating the cause of the death, but they say those who came into contact with the researcher all tested negative for pneumonic plague.

So what is pneumonic plague, and how dangerous is it?

Pneumonic plague is a really serious lung infection, often described as the most virulent form of plague.

There are two other types of plague: bubonic, which affects the lymph nodes; and septicaemic, which affects the blood.

Pneumonic plague can occur after an initial infection of one of these other types.

Symptoms include shortness of breath, chest pain, and often coughing up blood.

It's regarded as being more serious but less common than bubonic plague.

The global number of infections of all three types of plague varies each year, but it is probably somewhere between 1,000 to 3,000 cases.

Most of these are bubonic plague, and many of them occur in central Africa, but cases also develop in other places, including Russia, India, China, and the United States.

Prof Piero Olliaro is Professor of Poverty-Related Infectious Diseases at the University of Oxford.

He said: "Plague itself has not disappeared: the bacterium that causes it, Yersinia pestis , persists in animal reservoirs across many parts of the world.

"Around 200 rodent species can harbour the bacterium, with reservoirs found across the Americas, Eurasia and Africa.

"Sporadic human cases therefore continue to occur, but established surveillance, infection-control measures and effective antibiotic treatment are important tools for limiting their impact."

Plague is an infectious disease caused by bacteria usually found in small mammals and their fleas.

You can catch it by getting bitten by an infected flea or handling an infected animal.

But human-to-human transmission of pneumonic plague is also possible through coughing infected droplets into the air, which are then breathed in by another person, although this normally requires quite close contact.

You can also develop it if you have had septicaemic plague and the infection then spreads into the lungs.

It's thought that pneumonic plague was the main type of plague behind what is known as the Black Death, the massive outbreak that killed millions of people across Europe in the 14th Century.

Dr Zania Stamataki, Associate Professor of Viral Immunology at the University of Birmingham, says it is important that researchers are able to study diseases like plague.

"I understand why people find the idea of plague in a laboratory alarming, so it is worth saying why that work exists," she said.

"Plague is not a historical disease. It remains endemic in rodent populations across Africa, Asia and the Americas, and human cases occur every year, including outbreaks of the pneumonic form.

"Diagnostics, vaccine development and surveillance for antibiotic resistance all require laboratories that hold and study the live organism.

"This work is vital to prepare against outbreaks."

According to the World Health Organization, pneumonic plague has a very short incubation period - sometimes just 24 hours.

If it isn't diagnosed and then treated quickly, experts warn it is nearly always fatal.

But the good news is that plague responds well to antibiotics if the treatment starts early.

Dr Malick Gibani, Clinical Associate Professor in Bacterial Vaccinology at Imperial College London, says the infection is widely recognised as a serious threat to public health.

"Pneumonic plague is a very severe manifestation of plague disease.

"Some textbooks will say it has 100% mortality if left untreated, and it's difficult to have accurate figures in the modern age.

"It is treatable with antibiotics, particularly if started early.

"That's why anyone with high-risk potential exposure might be offered post-exposure prophylaxis with antibiotics and/or quarantine."

In the Russian case, it is still not yet clear whether the person who died was infected by pneumonic plague.

The authorities in Russia have issued a statement saying that tests had shown "no microorganisms associated with the patient's professional activities" – and so at this stage it is still not quite clear what has happened.

US President Donald Trump said Washington was looking "very strongly" at the case, while the Centers for Disease Control (CDC) said there was "no indication of a broader threat to the United States".

The UK's Health and Safety Authority said it was seeking more information, but that the risk to Britain's population was "very low".

articles.title: 'Making steady progress, regaining health': Indian embassy in UAE updates on flydubai pilot Smit Machchhar
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Captain Smit Machchhar is “making steady progress” and “regaining his health” after being seriously injured in an attack by his co-pilot on a
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Captain Smit Machchhar is “making steady progress” and “regaining his health” after being seriously injured in an attack by his co-pilot on a flydubai flight last week, the Indian Embassy in the UAE said on Tuesday.Machchhar was attacked by his co-pilot, an Omani national with a crash axe, an emergency tool typically kept in the cockpit during flydubai flight FZ1073 on Wednesday. The motive for the attack remains unclear.“Capt Smit continues to make steady progress and is regaining his health. The Embassy remains in close touch with his family, doctors & local authorities, extending all possible assistance,” the embassy said in a post on X.“We thank everyone for their prayers & wish him a speedy recovery,” it added.The flight, carrying 174 passengers, sent emergency signals after the attack and rapidly descended more than 17,000 feet from an altitude of 34,000 feet.Machchhar, who was lying injured on the cockpit floor, realised that the aircraft was descending and made “one last push” to open the cockpit door.He managed to activate the door release despite being seriously injured and covered in blood.Two reserve pilots then took control of the aircraft and landed it safely at Prince Sultan Bin Abdulaziz Airport in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia. The co-pilot was taken into custody, while Machchhar was taken to a nearby hospital for treatment.Machchhar was initially admitted to a hospital in Tabuk before being airlifted to Abu Dhabi for further medical treatment, PTI reported.On October 1, India's ambassador to the UAE, Deepak Mittal, had said Machchhar was “in good health and recovering well”. Mittal had also visited the injured captain and his family at the hospital.The investigation into the attack is ongoing, with the motive behind the co-pilot's actions still unclear.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: France explodes again as students riot over education
articles.summary: Video from France Tuesday shows protesters clashing with police and dodging tear gas as tens of thousands demand sweeping education reform nationwide.
articles.body: Violent scenes are emerging from France Tuesday as hundreds of thousands of people have taken to the streets to demand education reform, forcing the reported closure of more than half of the country's high schools. France's interior ministry said 6,100 people have been taken into custody since the protests began in September, while at least 715 police officers and 215 teenagers have been injured in clashes. Video taken in cities including Paris, Lyon and Strasbourg showed demonstrators facing off with police, lighting fires and dodging tear gas. In other areas, such as Marseille and Nantes, protesters held up signs with messages like, "The state has killed national education," Reuters reported. The Interior Ministry estimated that 256,000 people took part in the demonstrations nationwide, including 56,000 in Paris. Organizers had a higher count, claiming 450,000 were involved, including 100,000 in Paris, according to France24. The outlet, citing a government source, said French President Emmanuel Macron will meet with key ministers this evening to discuss the unrest. "What’s happening in France is nothing less than out of control mass migration. This isn’t about schools, this is about Islam wanting to take over a once great Country!" Trump wrote Tuesday on Truth Social. TEEN'S HAND BLOWN OFF BY POLICE GRENADE DURING FRENCH STUDENT PROTESTS: REPORT The protests are quickly blowing up as a hot topic in the election campaign to replace President Emmanuel Macron next May. Far-left presidential hopeful Jean-Luc Mélenchon has decried the government response to the protests as repressive. Critics have accused his party, La France Insoumise, (LFI), of seeking to use the unrest to score points in the presidential campaign and of inciting violence. Video previously posted to social media showed the Seine-Saint Denis mayor, Bally Bagayoko of the LFI, joining in with students, smiling and high-fiving pupils after a trash can was set on fire in the street. And the president of the Île‑de‑France region told Radio Monte Carlo, "There is a call to action being issued by LFI today: ‘Trash your high school.’ It is being spread via TikTok challenges." LFI has denied the accusations, according to Reuters. "This is a combination of the Islamists, together with the communists, the socialists, the far-left that are joining forces, and this is an outright uprising and insurrection basically is what it is that we are witnessing in France," Nile Gardiner, director of The Heritage Foundation's Margaret Thatcher Center for Freedom, told Fox News' "The Faulkner Focus" on Tuesday. "The stakes are incredibly high for the French people and this is a warning for the United States, as well." Authorities began shutting schools last week to try to defuse tensions after widespread damage to schools and mounting injuries among staff, students and police. Classes were totally or partially suspended Tuesday at 891 schools, according to the Education Ministry. The High School Students Union also told Reuters that over half of France's high schools were closed or blockaded Tuesday. Students have drawn attention to rundown classrooms that lack basics such as desks and chairs, become sweltering in summer without air conditioning and, in some cases, are infested with rats. Other common complaints include staff shortages and exhausting workloads. French high school students’ compulsory classroom hours are among the highest in Europe. "We want more money for the national educational system so that high schools are renovated," Roberta, a recent high school graduate in Paris, told Reuters. FRANCE ROCKED BY STUDENT RIOTS AS HUNDREDS ARRESTED, VIOLENCE SPREADS NATIONWIDE In one of the recent demonstrations in the town of Lens on Monday, a 15-year-old had picked up a police dispersal grenade that detonated, losing his hand and part of his lower arm, officials said. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has asked ministers in France to address student demands, including repairs to aging buildings, a call for longer lunch breaks and a review of the 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. school day, according to Reuters. Felix Barney, a university student, told The Associated Press that the police response was disproportionate. "It doesn’t have any sense to hit minors," he said. articles.title: Cleveland police pull body from water as they hunt for dad who vanished after Browns game
articles.summary: Phoenix Phillips, 24, vanished in downtown Cleveland hours after watching the Pittsburgh Steelers play. Police call the circumstances "concerning."
articles.body: A body was pulled from the water in Cleveland Tuesday afternoon as police searched for a Maryland father who vanished after traveling to the city for the Steelers-Browns game, though authorities have not confirmed whether the discovery is connected to his disappearance. Cleveland police spokesperson Sgt. Freddy Diaz told Fox News Digital the body was recovered shortly after 1 p.m. and will be taken to the Cuyahoga County Medical Examiner's Office for an autopsy. Phoenix Phillips, 24, was last seen at about 6 a.m. Friday in downtown Cleveland, the Cleveland Division of Police said in a missing-person alert. articles.title: Men jailed for raping teenage girl after grooming her on Snapchat
articles.summary: Three men tried to flee the UK in a lorry after their crimes, but were stopped by French police.
articles.body:
Three Afghan nationals who raped a teenager, before being stopped by French police as they fled the UK in the back of a lorry, have been jailed.

Mehrab Safi, 21, Awal Ahmadzai and Salman Habibkheli, both 19, were found guilty on 26 June of multiple offences against the girl at a house in St Werburghs, Bristol, last year.

Safi first met the 17-year-old girl, who cannot be named for legal reasons, while she was Christmas shopping, and groomed her over Snapchat before paying for a taxi to bring her to Bristol.

Safi was jailed for 15 years at Bristol Crown Court on Tuesday, while Habibkheli and Ahmadzai were both sentenced to nine years in a youth detention centre.

Sentencing the three men, Judge Michael Cullum said being trafficked and raped by the men will have caused "unimaginable" trauma to the teenager.

Warning: This story contains distressing details.

A 17-year-old boy - who is an Afghan national but cannot be named for legal reasons - was also convicted of rape, but he did not try to escape the UK. He was sentenced to two years and seven months in a youth detention centre.

In a victim impact statement read out to the court, the girl said the attack had left her "traumatised" and fearful of leaving the house.

If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line .

She added that she is a "different person" to who she was a year ago.

"I had a lot more friends, I would go out a lot more, I was happier. Now, I've stopped going out, I don't even leave the house in general.

"If I ever leave the house, it is only with my best friend or mum. I would not be able to go out by myself, even the thought of that makes me panic.

"Generally my brain keeps blocking out the trauma that happened to me, but when I am feeling low emotionally it all comes back and makes me feel even worse.

"Sometimes I would dream about what happened, which I was not expecting – and I do not like those dreams at all," she said.

Avon and Somerset Police said the girl, who was from Somerset, was plied with alcohol when she arrived at Safi's home. She was then sexually assaulted and raped over a number of hours by the three men and teenager in November last year.

Officers attended the property and found the girl after her mother reported her missing.

Det Sgt Jo Babbage said the victim had begun communicating with Safi five days before the attacks "via mobile, predominantly Snapchat".

She said: "It's clear that that's where the grooming and the contact process was started that led up to her being brought into Bristol by taxi which was arranged [by Safi]."

Babbage said the girl has been left "very traumatised" by the attacks, but has been "very brave" throughout the investigation.

The victim came to Bristol for the first time on 25 November 2025 with a friend on a Christmas shopping trip.

During the trip, the girl met Safi and they exchanged numbers and Snapchat contacts.

Safi later used the platform to persuade her to send nude photos.

He then arranged for a taxi to take her from her home to his house in St Werburghs in the early hours of 30 November where he and the three others carried out the attacks.

Babbage said: "Just hearing that, reading it, this Christmas shopping trip that ended like that, as a parent, makes you feel terrified for your children to go out."

The 17-year-old boy was arrested at the scene, but the three men fled from officers and travelled to Birmingham and London before they left the country in a lorry.

They were discovered by French police in Calais and returned to the UK where they were immediately arrested on suspicion of rape.

Babbage said: "They got into the back of a lorry... and they were able to leave the country without documents and it was just fortuitous that our friends in France located them and were able to return them straight away."

Mobile phone footage from Safi's phone showed the men laughing and gesticulating in the back of the lorry, which the prosecution said during the trial had suggested they thought they had "got away with it".

Sentencing the men and teenager, Judge Cullum said the victim would have looked "vulnerable from the very beginning".

"I have no doubt that was her attraction to you, Safi. After an intense exchange of texts you obtained nude photos of her.

"Reading of the exchanges is uncomfortable and starts to suggest an imbalance of power between you [Safi] and the victim.

"Having been trafficked she was raped five times, and cumulative trauma will undoubtedly live with her forever and is unimaginable," he said.

During sentencing, the judge acknowledged the traumatic experiences all four had endured in Afghanistan. The judge also noted that one of them had lost a parent at the hands of the Taliban.

However, he said that this was no excuse.

All four were also sentenced to be put on the sex offender's register indefinitely, and received a sexual harm prevention order which stops them communicating with children.

articles.title: In 2026, a homeless former clothing reseller pulled discarded office chairs from a Nashville dumpster, made a $17,000 profit and later built a six-figure resale business
articles.summary: Explore the inspiring story of a former clothing reseller who transformed his life by dumpster diving for discarded office chairs, turning a $17,000 profit and growing his business to six figures by 2026.
articles.body: What looks useless to one person can be an inventory to another. After realising that discarded items could still hold significant value, a former apparel reseller in Nashville turned this idea into a business. Office furniture was his breakthrough: after seeing a large number of unwanted chairs, he realised that goods companies discard can be resold instead of wasted. The 190 Steelcase chairs from that haul brought in roughly $17,000. His finances improved after that discovery, and by 2026 his larger dumpster-resale business was generating six figures.The chairs changed his businessBefore that, Carter Stevens was a vintage clothing reseller in Nashville. That business taught him how to price used stuff, how to find buyers, and that the worth of an item depends on who is looking for it, not on whether the original owner still wants it. When that business dried up, his financial circumstances deteriorated, and he ultimately became homeless. Dumpster diving began as a way to find items to sell rather than as a conventional business model.The office chairs made the difference. Stevens salvaged 190 Steelcase office chairs from a warehouse in Nashville. They were not broken, and the Steelcase name carried recognisable value in the secondhand market. He brought them back, then cleaned and listed them for sale. Over around six weeks, the haul netted nearly $17,000 in profit, while his wider eBay sales brought in about $30,000 in revenue. He built on that model, and by 2026 his larger resale business was generating six figures.From dumpster finds to a resale businessStevens began to recover more than just furniture. He looked around Nashville for clothes, electronics, and home items, some of which he could resell online instead of tossing. But finding the goods was only part of the work. Bulky products need to be carried, photographed, stored, cleaned when needed and matched with customers. For someone dealing with dumpsters instead of a normal wholesaler, shipping and storage can be as crucial as the resale price.He had a model for that approach in the office-chair haul. He could recognise things with recognisable labels, determine their secondhand value and reach beyond the people immediately around him via online marketplaces. His later income did not come from one lucky find. The six-figure figure reflects the growth of the business into a larger resale operation.That distinction matters because a $17,000 profit from a single haul is extraordinary. It does not mean every discarded office chair is valuable or that dumpster diving automatically becomes a viable income source. The business can work when resale value exceeds the costs and risks of recovering the goods.The resale economy behind the storyStevens' experience fits the logic of the circular economy: an item one owner discards can still serve another buyer. Reuse can extend a product's life and postpone a replacement purchase. A 2025 review of studies on secondhand clothing and the circular economy concluded that resale can prolong product use and support circular consumption, but the environmental effect is contingent upon the fate of the original product and what new purchase the used item substitutes. The same approach can apply beyond apparel to furniture and electronics.That does not mean that all types of resale are automatically viable. Transport, storage and packing, and customer behaviour influence the outcome. But a chair, television or piece of clothes that is still serviceable usually takes a different route to disposal than just throwing it away. For Stevens, the idea for a circular economy became a business opportunity, not a formal sustainability effort.The spending problem was part of the storyThis is a change from his past financial struggles. He experienced a cycle of heavy spending without much financial security, followed by a period in which discarded goods became a source of income rather than spending. A longitudinal study in Psychiatry Research linked compulsive shopping to a lower quality of life and higher financial costs among people followed from adolescence to midlife.Another five-year follow-up study of individuals diagnosed with compulsive shopping disorder indicated that some participants had a drop in shopping and spending symptoms over time, but triggers such as boredom, negative feelings and pressure could lead to the behaviour returning. Those studies did not examine Stevens and cannot explain his particular situation. They do suggest why shifting the direction of money, from buying undesired items to discovering value in unwanted things, can make such a huge difference in a personal financial story.What the dumpster experiment really showsThe notable part of Stevens' story is that he saw a recurring market where others saw disposability. The proof of concept was the 190 office chairs. His history in garment resale gave him insight into how secondhand markets worked, and the $17,000 profit on one haul made the case for continuing the quest. By 2026 the model had become a six-figure earner. For Stevens, the dumpster was not the end of a product's life but the start of a second market.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Hilarious animal photos from this year’s Comedy Wildlife Awards
articles.summary: Some of the cutest, weirdest and most comedic animal photographs and videos of the year have been released.
articles.body: Some of the cutest, weirdest and most comedic animal photographs and videos of the year have been released. Perhaps an elephant covering an eye with his trunk, as if participating in a game of hide and seek, makes you gush. Or two birds face-to-face in close proximity, covering themselves with their wings as if to share a secret kiss away from prying eyes, could evoke a giggle. Maybe two bears joking around make you chuckle. Or a green mantis seemingly posing like a model for a sexy photo shoot on a leaf makes you smile. These scenes were all captured in creative images that made the final of the 2026 Nikon Comedy Wildlife Awards. A heart-warming shortlist of 47 images and nine videos were selected from more than 10,000 submissions from 112 countries – the most entries in the annual competition’s 11-year history, according to organizers. The light-hearted competition was created in 2015 in a bid to use humor to promote wildlife conservation. “The Comedy Wildlife Photography Awards started very gently, somewhere out on the vast plains of the Serengeti,” competition co-founder Tom Sullam said in a statement. “What began as a small effort to raise awareness of wildlife conservation has grown into something far bigger than we ever imagined.” “The competition is now truly global, and a decade or so on, we want to make it even bigger, funnier, and more far-reaching than ever,” he added. “We use humour to get people to feel empathy towards wildlife, and it’s that empathy that creates behavioural change for the better.” If you want to look through all the hilarious and charming finalists, and pick your favorite, voting is now open for the STERNA People’s Choice Award. The final winners, decided by a judging panel, will be announced at an awards night in London on December 8. Finalists’ works will then be exhibited until December 13. articles.title: The Netherlands built two 210-metre gates to hold back the North Sea; they can close automatically when storm surges threaten Zuid-Holland
articles.summary: In the Netherlands, two enormous gates, each 210 metres wide, can close against the North Sea to hold back dangerous storm surges.
articles.body: In the Netherlands, two enormous gates, each 210 metres wide, can close against the North Sea to hold back dangerous storm surges. Known as the Maeslant Barrier, the structure stands near Hoek van Holland and was built between 1991 and 1997. According to Rijkswaterstaat, the Dutch agency that manages it, no other flood barrier in the world has larger moving parts. The barrier closes fully automatically when water levels are forecast to rise dangerously, and it helps protect residents of the province of Zuid-Holland. This article explains how it works, what it measures, and who keeps it ready and tested.How the Maeslant Barrier near Hoek van Holland protects Zuid-Holland from North Sea storm surgesMinistry of Infrastructure and Water Management, Rijkswaterstaat, describes Maeslant Barrier as a vital part of the Delta Works, the Dutch system of flood defences. It is designed to withstand a storm surge of 5 metres above a reference level that roughly equals the average sea level in the North Sea. The barrier sits in the New Waterway and is a forward flood surge barrier, which means it takes the full force of the tidal surge coming in from the sea. Together with the Hartel Barrier and the extended Rozenburg Dyke, it forms the Europoort Barrier.How the barrier was designed and built between 1991 and 1997Rijkswaterstaat explains that the Maeslant Barrier was not part of the original Delta Plan, yet its design is just as ingenious and massive as the other Delta Works structures. Before construction, an independent committee examined four options for the barrier, working closely with Rijkswaterstaat, the municipality of Rotterdam, and the water authority. The committee weighed cost, building time, the effect on the economy, and how well the barrier would blend into the landscape. Construction ran from 1991 to 1997, and the barrier was closed for the first time in 2007.How two gates, each 210 metres wide, fill with water and sink within two hoursAccording to the Keringhuis water information centre in Hoek van Holland, the barrier has two gates, each 210 metres wide, 22 metres high, and 15 metres deep. Rijkswaterstaat explains that when the barrier closes, the gates fill with water and sink to the bottom, and the Keringhuis says the whole closing takes two hours. The structure turns on ball-and-socket joints, each 10 metres in diameter and weighing 680 tons. Both organisations state that no other flood barrier in the world has larger moving parts. Rijkswaterstaat also uses a specially developed model to calculate the risk that the barrier fails to close.How the Maeslant Barrier closes fully automatically, when it has closed, and when operators step inRijkswaterstaat says the barrier closes automatically when the water level near Rotterdam is predicted to rise more than 3 metres above the reference level, or more than 2.9 metres near Dordrecht, and that "No human intervention is required." An operational team is still on hand to monitor and step in if needed. The Keringhuis reports that the barrier closed on 21 December 2023 for the first time at its official threshold, when the Rotterdam forecast reached 3 metres. It had twice closed earlier at a lowered threshold of 2.6 metres, in November 2007 and January 2018. In storms in 2002, 2013, and 2014 it came within a few centimetres of closing. Visitors can learn more at the Keringhuis.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: In 2011, an Australian janitor found A$100,000 stuffed into a TV station toilet; after nobody claimed it, he was awarded A$81,597
articles.summary: In a surprising turn of events in 2011, an Australian cleaner found over A$100,000 cash hidden in a toilet at Channel Nine in Melbourne, leading to a three-year mystery and a court ruling awarding him nearly A$81,597 of the funds.
articles.body: A routine cleaning shift at an Australian television station took an extraordinary turn in 2011 when a cleaner discovered more than A$100,000 hidden inside a toilet. The cash was found at Channel Nine’s Melbourne headquarters, sparking a three-year mystery over who left it there. According to SBS News, cleaner Chamindu Amarsinghe did not walk away with the money after discovering it. He reported the cash to his supervisor, who contacted police. Some of the money was found inside a sanitary bin, while additional notes were recovered from the plumbing. No one came forward to claim the cash, leaving investigators with more than A$100,000 and no established owner.The strange discoveryAmarsinghe was cleaning the toilets on the ground floor of Channel Nine's Melbourne headquarters when he saw something strange in one of the sanitary bins. There were bundles of Australian currency notes in the bin. Amarsinghe found the money so unusual that he initially thought it might have been a hoax. The police arrived at the scene, and after finding out that some money had been found in the bathroom plumbing, a plumber was summoned. This raised questions about where the money came from and who had left it there. However, despite all attempts to establish the rightful owner of the money, no claim was put forward.A mystery that lasted yearsAs reported by The Guardian, the money stayed with the authorities while attempts were being made to trace the source. At one point, a Sydney man was charged in connection with possible proceeds of crime, but the charge was soon dropped. In the end, investigators could not determine who had put the money there. Since no owner came forward, it became clear that the matter would end up in court. Almost three years after the discovery of the money, a Melbourne magistrate had to decide on its fate. At this point, Amarsinghe was already living in New Zealand, where he was pursuing his education in information technology. He continued working and studying, apparently without expecting to recover the money.By then, the question was no longer just about who had left the cash in the toilet. With no one coming forward to claim it, the court had to decide what would happen to the money and whether Amarsinghe should receive any of it. The ruling would finally bring the unusual case to a close, even though the mystery of who left the cash behind remained unsolved.The cleaner gets most of the moneyMelbourne Magistrates' Court magistrate Michael Smith awarded Amarsinghe A$81,597 of the money he had found. About A$19,500 was retained by the state. The decision rewarded the cleaner for reporting the cash and helping authorities investigate its origins. Police supported the decision, while the court noted that Amarsinghe had done the right thing when he discovered the money. What began as an ordinary shift ended with a life-changing sum.Amarsinghe said he was speechless when he learned about the decision. He planned to use the money to support his future, including his career in information technology. He also said he wanted to donate some of it to help disabled people and to a Buddhist temple. The biggest mystery, however, remained unanswered. Even after more than three years, investigators could not determine who had hidden the cash in the television station's toilet or why it had been left there. For Amarsinghe, the story had an unusual ending. The discovery began with a toilet full of unexplained cash and ended with a court awarding him A$81,597.You use AI every day. articles.title: Miami Beach’s Savoy Hotel dates to the 1930s and survived decades on Ocean Drive; Florida laws could now allow most of it and the neighboring Arlington to be demolished for a 38-story, 480-foot tower
articles.summary: The Savoy Hotel has stood on Miami Beach’s Ocean Drive since 1937, a low-rise Art Deco landmark in a neighbourhood defined by that style.
articles.body: The Savoy Hotel has stood on Miami Beach’s Ocean Drive since 1937, a low-rise Art Deco landmark in a neighbourhood defined by that style. Now, a plan filed by Allied Partners would demolish most of the Savoy and the neighbouring Arlington Hotel to make way for a 38-story, 480-foot tower designed by Arquitectonica. The project relies on Florida’s Live Local Act to bypass local zoning limits and on the Resiliency and Safe Structures Act to allow demolition of flood-vulnerable historic buildings, according to WLRN and project filings. Read on to know more details here:A landmark from the 1930sThe Savoy Hotel was built in 1937, during the era when Miami Beach’s Ocean Drive was taking shape as a showcase for Art Deco architecture. Its low-rise footprint and distinctive facade have made it a familiar sight in the South of Fifth neighbourhood for nearly a century. The neighbouring Arlington Hotel, built in 1941, shares the block and has been closed since it was badly damaged by Hurricane Irma. Under the current proposal, the Arlington would be demolished entirely, while the Savoy would lose most of its structure. What remains would be the hotel’s lobby and a small section of its Ocean Drive facade, both of which would be retained and restored intact. The developer says the new building’s street front is designed to match the scale of the two old hotels and sit in line with the preserved elements, as per Oftmw.com.That partial preservation is a compromise that has drawn criticism from preservation advocates. Meg Lousteau, executive director of the Miami Design Preservation League, told WLRN that the loss of most of the Savoy would damage the city’s iconic brand and image. She warned that the combination of state laws could lead to wholesale changes in how many parts of Miami Beach feel at street level.How Florida’s Live Local Act enables the towerThe Live Local Act, passed in 2023, allows developers to sidestep many local zoning regulations when building large structures. Under the law, a project can qualify for the highest density and tallest height within a one-mile radius if at least 40 percent of its units are maintained as workforce housing for at least 30 years. This provision is what makes a 38-story tower possible on a strip known for its low-rise Art Deco and Mid-Century Modern buildings, as per WLRN NPR News.The proposed Savoy tower would rise about 480 feet, or 453 feet depending on the measurement cited in filings, well above the surrounding buildings. It would include 90 market-rate condominiums averaging 2,851 square feet, 60 workforce rental units in the parking podium, and a 76-key hotel. The workforce rentals would be restricted to households earning at or below 120 percent of area median income for at least 30 years, as per Oftmw.com.Reports further suggest that the project also calls for 257 parking spaces, a sixth-floor pool deck, a beachfront hotel restaurant, and a beach club. The mix of uses reflects a broader trend in Miami Beach development, where residential towers increasingly incorporate hotel and retail components. The Live Local Act’s density and height provisions make such projects financially viable in areas where local zoning would otherwise limit them.The Resiliency and Safe Structures Act and demolitionThe Resiliency and Safe Structures Act, passed in 2024, is the other key piece of legislation enabling the project. The law bars local governments in coastal communities from preventing the demolition of historic structures that do not meet modern flood standards or have been deemed unsafe. It also prevents local governments from requiring the preservation of any elements of a demolished structure.Almost all of Miami Beach falls within a FEMA flood zone, which means many older buildings qualify under the law’s criteria. The Savoy Hotel sits in the South of Fifth neighbourhood, just outside the Miami Beach Architectural District, which was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1979. That placement matters because the law includes an exception for historic properties within districts recognised before January 1, 2000, and the Savoy falls outside that boundary.Miami Beach Commissioner Alex Fernandez told WLRN that the city has been stripped of its authority to stop the demolition of historic properties like the Savoy and Arlington. He described the situation as a horrible state preemption that affects every coastal community in Florida. The city still has limited authority to review plans, but that authority has been diluted under the new laws.Community pushback and the limits of local controlResidents and local officials have pushed back against the project, but their options are constrained by state preemption. The Miami Design Preservation League had warned as early as 2024 that the Resiliency and Safe Structures Act could lead to the demolition of the Savoy and other historic properties. Lousteau told WLRN that the outcome was predictable and predicted, and that the combination of the two laws could reshape the character of Miami Beach.Community activism did succeed in blocking an earlier version of the demolition bill in 2023, but the legislation passed the following year. Commissioner Fernandez said the current situation is the fulfilment of a prophecy, with everything opponents warned about now happening. He noted that the city’s hands are tied and that residents have virtually no way to stop the demolition under the current legal framework.The debate reflects a broader tension between state-level development policy and local preservation efforts. Florida’s coastal cities face pressure to build more housing and improve resilience, but critics argue that the current laws remove too much local control. For Miami Beach, the Savoy case has become a symbol of that tension.What comes next for the Savoy siteThe project is still in the planning and review stage, with construction not yet underway. Allied Partners filed a letter of intent in April 2026 invoking the Live Local Act, and the plans have since been filed with the city. The developer, Savoy Hotel Partners LLC, is owned by Allied Partners CEO Eric D. Hadar and family.If the project moves forward, the new tower would bring a significant change to Ocean Drive’s skyline. The 38-story building would stand in sharp contrast to the low-rise Art Deco character that has defined the street for decades. Whether the partial preservation of the Savoy’s lobby and facade will be enough to satisfy preservation advocates remains to be seen.For now, the Savoy’s future hangs on the interplay between two state laws and the limits they place on local authority. The case highlights how development pressure, flood risk, and historic preservation can collide in coastal cities. As Miami Beach continues to evolve, the Savoy may become a test case for how much of the city’s architectural heritage can be retained under Florida’s current legal framework.You use AI every day. articles.title: What would it take for the Yemen offensive to succeed?
articles.summary: Territorial gains alone will not be enough to change the trajectory of the war.
articles.body:
Two days after the announced counter-offensive by the internationally recognised Yemeni government, the operation named Dawn of Yemen has already made significant advances. Its forces recaptured territory from the Houthis, an Iran-backed group, along the Red Sea coast near the Bab al-Mandeb strait.

The Saudi-led coalition backing the government has deployed 100 fighter jets, flying round-the-clock to help secure the strait. In response, the Houthis have claimed attacks on Saudi territory.

This is the most consequential escalation in the Yemen war since the UN-brokered truce of 2022. For four years, the war was managed as a frozen conflict. Now, both sides are trying to redraw the map.

In the coming days, the success of the offensive will be determined not only by gains along three different fronts, but also by the ability of the forces loyal to the Yemeni government to maintain cohesion and force the Houthis to change their cost of conflict calculus.

The western coast is where the campaign will be won or lost, and the reason lies beyond Yemen. With Iran disrupting traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea has become the Gulf’s strategic lifeline. Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline to Yanbu is its main route around Hormuz, yet crude shipped from Yanbu to Asian markets must still pass through Bab al-Mandeb.

A Houthi grip on the strait’s Yemeni shore turns that bypass into a hostage. The Arabian Peninsula would then be squeezed at both ends simultaneously, a scenario that no Gulf capital, and few oil importing economies, can tolerate for long.

There is also a counterintuitive point here. The Houthis’ greatest gain of the year – the territories near Bab al-Mandeb – may also be their most exposed position. Their traditional strength lies in the mountains of the north, where terrain, tribal networks and short supply lines favour defence.

The Tihama coast is the opposite: a flat plain, far from their highland base, with long and vulnerable supply routes and little cover from sustained airpower.

If the government can win decisively anywhere, it is here. The immediate aim need not be to defeat the Houthis outright, but to push them back from the strait, retake the islands and deny them the ability to convert geography into regional leverage.

The second decisive front is Taiz. The city is the hinge between the Houthi-held north, the government-held south and the western coastal theatre. If the Houthis keep the Aden road severed, any broader offensive is split in two. If government forces reopen it, they gain territorial continuity between Aden, Taiz and the coast.

The third is Marib governorate, where fighting has escalated on the Raghwan front, and potentially al-Jawf.

Despite sweeping rhetoric from the Yemeni government, an early march on Sanaa remains unlikely. The more plausible strategy is cumulative pressure: if the coast, Taiz and Marib are pressed at the same time, the Houthis will struggle to concentrate manpower, missiles, drones and logistics on any single axis. The government does not need breakthroughs everywhere; it needs to keep the Houthis overstretched.

The government has rarely lacked external backers. Its recurring failure has been converting that support into coherent Yemeni military power. Saudi Arabia remains decisive, and its incentives are now direct rather than abstract: Aramco facilities are under fire, Saudi-linked shipping has been declared a target and the main route circumventing the Strait of Hormuz is exposed.

The commitment of 100 aircraft signals that Riyadh is willing to invest heavily.

Airpower can destroy positions, cut supply lines and break concentrations of force, but it cannot hold territory. That requires Yemeni forces to fight under a unified chain of command, support functioning local administration and maintain political agreement that prevents infighting between factions.

Here the anti-Houthi camp is arguably weaker than at any point in the war. The Southern Transitional Council, which launched its own offensive across the south in December 2025, was dissolved in January after a Saudi-backed counteroffensive, and its leader, Aidarous al-Zubaidi, left the country. The southern units that fought under its banner remain armed and capable, but without a political roof, and their loyalty to the Yemeni government is conditional.

Alongside them, Tareq Saleh’s National Resistance on the coast, the Southern Giants Brigades, and units aligned with the Islah Party in Taiz and Marib each answer to different leaderships, regional priorities and external patrons.

The Houthis, by contrast, possess a centralised political and military command.

This asymmetry is the offensive’s greatest vulnerability. If it is fought through fragmented chains of command, gains will be temporary: rival forces will compete over captured territory, revenues and authority, and the Houthis will regroup and counterattack.

Recognising this reality, the Yemeni government has started preparing to hand out salary payments and undertake reconstruction in recovered areas. That is the right instinct. A town taken by airstrikes but left unpaid and ungoverned will not stay taken. This effort needs to be maintained.

The offensive should not be judged by whether it captures Sanaa. That benchmark is maximalist and almost guarantees a verdict of failure. The better question is whether it makes the conflict ripe for resolution.

In the language of conflict studies, parties negotiate seriously when they perceive a mutually hurting impasse. Since 2022, the deadlock has hurt the Yemeni people, the government, Saudi Arabia and global shipping, but not the Houthis, who have had every reason to believe that time works in their favour. The purpose of Dawn of Yemen, properly understood, is not total victory, but a change in the Houthis’ assessment of the costs of continued confrontation.

There is a complication. The Houthis’ calculus is no longer purely Yemeni. Their decisions are now entangled with Tehran’s war and its bargaining with Washington. Even significant battlefield losses may not produce flexibility in the group if its leadership believes concessions should be traded within a wider regional deal. A specifically Yemeni settlement may therefore depend partly on movement in a negotiation that Yemenis do not control.

Over the coming weeks, four indicators will tell us which way the war is turning: whether government forces retake and hold the coast and the strait islands; whether the Taiz-Aden road is reopened; whether the Houthis are forced to pull forces from Taiz to defend the coast and Marib; and whether recovered areas come under a single command and receive salaries and services.

If most of these happen, the strategic geometry of the war may shift. If government forces advance only marginally, suffer heavy losses or turn on one another, the Houthis will claim to have survived yet another externally backed campaign, and that narrative will harden their conviction that they can outlast their opponents.

All of this unfolds amid a deepening humanitarian catastrophe. The World Health Organization has recorded more than 5,000 casualties since early August, while nearly 200,000 people have been displaced and suspected cholera cases have tripled. A campaign that ignores this will exhaust international patience quickly, as happened with the operation to recapture Hodeidah in 2018, when government forces were pressured to stop to avert a humanitarian disaster.

The offensive then is not the turning point itself. It is the opening of a test. The Yemeni government must do what it has struggled to do throughout this war: convert external support into unified political authority and sustainable military power. If it fails, the Houthis will emerge from another round more convinced than ever that time remains on their side.

articles.title: In 2021, Spain mixed ash from waste paper and sludge into a one-kilometre peri-urban road; its roadbed met the country's highest required E3 class
articles.summary: In a groundbreaking project, Spain successfully utilized Waste Paper Fly Ash to create a durable road, surpassing national standards for structural integrity and sustainability.
articles.body: A Spanish road project used Waste Paper Fly Ash (WPFA), a residue derived from paper rejects and sludge, as a substitute for cement in a stabilized road subgrade. Built in Villamayor de Gállego in Zaragoza, the pilot covered a 1,000-metre-long and 5.7-metre-wide section of a peri-urban road. As testing showed, the WPFA-stabilized layer achieved an average static modulus above 334 MPa, the highest class specified for the section, and exceeded the 300 MPa threshold for the E3 subgrade category.The work was part of the EU-funded Paper Chain project, which examined whether WPFA could work as a hydraulic binder, replacing conventional cement work for stabilizing soils used beneath road pavements. Having previously investigated WPFA at laboratory scale and in other field trials, the researchers, however, focused on the construction and monitoring of one Spanish pilot. Although the road section didn’t carry high intensity of traffic, it was used by agricultural vehicles and trucks travelling to a local service area. The WPFA solution replaced a cement-stabilized soil classified as S-EST3 under Spanish road regulations, with a double bituminous treatment over the improved subgrade.For the laboratory mix, the researchers determined that the stabilized soil should contain 5% WPFA and 8.2% water, while the reference mixture contained 3% CEM IV/B (Q) 32.5N cement and 7% water. Unlike the cement mixture, the WPFA mixture required a 30-minute delay before compaction, followed by compaction to the maximum Modified Proctor dry density.The WPFA layer reached the required strength and subgrade classLaboratory specimens made from the WPFA mixture reached an average 1.8 MPa against the minimum requirement of 1.5 MPa and met the Spanish requirement for seven-day unconfined compressive strength. The stiffness of the completed layer was assessed through load-plate tests and in 14 days the WPFA section recorded an average Ev2 above 334 MPa. According to the study, the Spanish regulations required thresholds of more than 60 MPa for E1, more than 120 MPa for E2 and more than 300 MPa for E3. The measured value therefore placed the WPFA-stabilized roadbed in the E3 category.Construction involved the removal of 10 centimetres of the original surface layer which was replaced with borrowed soil. Using a dosing machine the WPFA was spread and mixed with the underlying soil to a depth of 25 centimetres. The mixture was compacted using four passes of a vibratory roller, followed by grading and a final static roller pass, before the double bituminous treatment was applied.After construction, technical inspections continued. Six months after its completion, no damage associated with the WPFA was identified. The second inspection came 15 months after completion and described the pavement in good condition overall, with only minor defects, such as potholes and loose aggregates, unrelated to the stabilization. The cement reference section, meanwhile, showed transverse cracks at four-metre intervals, while no cracking or swelling was observed in the WPFA section.Environmental monitoring tracked leaching and material stabilityResearchers also sampled the construction materials, surrounding soils, vegetation, groundwater and nearby surface waters before and after construction. The monitoring plan examined potential pathways for WPFA particles and focused on airborne dispersion during spreading and water transport via runoff. The concentrations of trace elements found in soils and dust collected from vegetation were similar before and after construction and no conclusive evidence was gathered by the researchers pertaining to the dispersal of WPFA through the identified construction pathways. Furthermore, all measured concentration remained below the threshold limits established for urban use soils in Aragon.Except for antimony, leaching tests indicated that the WPFA-stabilized material met the criteria for inert waste. However, leachate collected from piezometers after heavy rainfall showed very low metal mobility, while in the percolation test all metals remained below the inert-waste thresholds. Two years post-construction, follow-up plate-load tests found that the average static modulus of the WPFA section had reached 336 MPa, reportedly a 17% rise. The researchers concluded that WPFA could serve as an alternative hydraulic binder, but cautioned against using it in soils with high sulfate to avoid ettringite formation.You use AI every day. articles.title: Jury selection begins for Ohio father charged with murdering deputy with car after son killed by police
articles.summary: Jury selection is underway in the murder trial of Rodney L. Hinton, the Ohio father accused of striking a deputy with his vehicle hours after viewing body camera footage of a Cincinnati police officer fatally shooting his son.
articles.body: Jury selection is underway in the murder trial of Rodney L. Hinton, the Ohio father accused of striking a deputy with his vehicle hours after viewing body camera footage of a Cincinnati police officer fatally shooting his son. Judge Jody Luebbers has called 107 potential jurors, NBC affiliate WLWT of Cincinnati reported. Jury selection began Monday and is expected to resume Tuesday. Hinton’s attorney, Clyde Bennett II, told the news station that he wants to make sure the seated jury can put aside their opinions and preconceived notions about the case and “follow the law given by Judge Luebbers.” “That’s going to be difficult,” he said. “I’m looking for 12 individuals from Hamilton County that can be fair and impartial, notwithstanding the fact that you have a very valued, loved deputy that was killed in the line of duty for no reason,” Bennett continued. According to the news station, the jury selection process includes a 23-page questionnaire and days of questioning by attorneys. More than a dozen potential jurors have already been dismissed, WLWT reported. Bennett did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Tuesday. Hinton, 40, was indicted on two counts of aggravated murder, murder, and two counts of felonious assault after prosecutors said he intentionally used his vehicle to run down and kill Hamilton County special deputy Larry Henderson in May 2025. Henderson retired from the Hamilton County Sheriff’s Office about five months before his death and was working as a special deputy directing traffic near the University of Cincinnati during graduation. Hours before the incident, Hinton had watched body camera video of his 18-year-old son, Ryan Hinton, being fatally shot by a Cincinnati officer responding to a report of a stolen vehicle at an apartment complex. Family said Hinton was “upset” and “agitated.” Theresa Larkin, Ryan Hinton’s aunt, previously told NBC News that it was extremely difficult to watch the video. “I can only imagine what he felt when he saw that video,” she said in an interview last year. “Because when I finally seen it, and I watched that video from the beginning to the end and watched my nephew drop, it was like my soul left my body. So I can only imagine how his father felt.” Police said that Ryan Hinton was among a group of people in an allegedly stolen car. Some people in the group ran after officers approached them, authorities said. Two officers pursued Ryan Hinton, who police said was armed, and another person. In video released by police, an officer was seen exiting his vehicle and pointing his gun at Ryan Hinton, who appeared to be running away. The officer fired at least four times, police said at a press conference last year. In another video, an officer could be heard yelling, “He’s got a gun!” Authorities said the gun was recovered at the scene. During a chaotic bond hearing last year that ended with Hinton being escorted from the courtroom following a commotion in the gallery, police said that concerned relatives drove Hinton from the police station after he watched the video. He later returned to the station to pick up his vehicle from the parking lot, authorities said. Police said that after leaving the parking lot, Hinton drove toward the university and appeared to stop before he allegedly “accelerated quickly” through an intersection where the deputy was standing. Police said there was no indication that Hinton tried to stop. In December, Hinton changed his plea from not guilty to not guilty by reason of insanity. A forensic psychologist appointed by the court said during the hearing that Hinton has bipolar disorder. Bennett said his client’s mental illness significantly affected his decision-making the day Henderson died. The plea change made him ineligible for the death penalty under Ohio law.

articles.title: Cervical screening: Family of woman who died after 'misread' test calls for public inquiry
articles.summary: Relatives of Louise Corbett Gibbons support the campaign for an inquiry into screening services.
articles.body:
The family of a 24-year-old woman who died after her smear test was said to have been misread has supported calls for a public inquiry into Northern Ireland's cervical screening service.

Louise Corbett Gibbons, from near Katesbridge in County Down, died from cervical cancer in 2008.

Her death is not linked to the cervical screening scandal involving the Southern Health Trust but her widower Neville Gibbons and aunt Joy Fairley joined campaigners to mark three years since those issues came to light.

The Southern Trust scandal led to 17,500 women being approached to have their smear tests rechecked as part of a major review of screening dating back to 2008.

Campaigners calling themselves the Ladies with Letters have since been calling for a statutory public inquiry into what went wrong.

They also argue that while the scandal involved the Southern Trust, other health trusts in Northern Ireland could have been affected.

17,500 cervical smear tests to be re-checked

Reports provide 'no outcome' for women impacted by misread smear tests

Campaign 'far from over' as minister rules out cervical screening inquiry

Gibbons told BBC News NI that when Louise received her diagnosis she was told she would "be gone within the month".

He said the pair, who had been together for eight years, got married the following week. Louise died three weeks later.

He said the wedding was "the saddest day of my life".

"Like, watching your wife in a wheelchair and knowing she's going to be dead in a few weeks," he said.

"My mind wasn't good for a very long time."

He said when the Southern Trust screening scandal came to light, it brought back many difficult memories.

He said Louise's family had been told that her smear had been misread but that "she would have passed away anyway".

That was something he said the family could not accept.

"I think she was never given the chance to start off with," he said.

Louise was a patient of the Belfast Health Trust. BBC News NI has written to the trust for comment.

Enda McGarrity, a solicitor for the Ladies with Letters, said there were "many women" from outside the Southern Trust who had been affected by cervical screening issues.

He said the renewed call by the Ladies with Letters for a public inquiry therefore went beyond the Southern Trust, which he said had "illuminated things much more clearly".

"But there was a cervical screening programme throughout Northern Ireland during that period," he said.

"So at the very least, there should be an investigation into whether these issues were replicated in other trusts.

"At this stage it's an issue where there is a concern that there's a link between those and how the cervical screening programme actually performed throughout those years and at the least it merits further investigation."

Earlier this year, former Health Minister Mike Nesbitt ruled out a public inquiry into failings in Northern Ireland's cervical screening service.

Heather Thompson and Tracey Bell were among the Ladies with Letters who took to the steps of Stormont on Tuesday, alongside a number of cross-party assembly members, to renew their calls for a public inquiry.

Thompson said that when the group became aware of Louise's death, it hit members "very hard".

She said the group feared there could be "other ladies out there" with similar experiences.

Tracey Bell said the group was to meet Health Minister Robbie Butler next month and that it was hopeful he would "listen carefully to the experiences of women and families affected" and "recognise why this matter could not be considered closed".

articles.title: Kenya confirms first Ebola case as man dies in Nairobi after DRC return
articles.summary: More than 4,000 people have died in the worst outbreak in the DR Congo’s history, with confirmed cases surpassing 8,300.
articles.body:
Kenya has confirmed its ‌‌first Ebola case after the death of a Kenyan national in Nairobi, who had returned from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC).

The patient, who had lived in the DRC for seven years, had been ill for about a month before travelling by road from the DRC to Uganda’s capital, Kampala, and then flying to ⁠⁠Nairobi on Saturday, Aden Duale, Kenya’s health secretary, told a news conference on Tuesday.

Seeking to halt local transmission, Kenya’s President William Ruto said at least eight family members of the victim and 21 healthcare workers have been quarantined, as he ordered an enhanced response to contain the virus in the country.

Earlier, Health Secretary Duale said 28 contacts, including family members and health workers who cared for the patient, had been identified. Another 23 passengers and four crew members who travelled on the same flight from Uganda were being traced.

Patrick Amoth, director-general of the Kenyan Ministry of Health, said the contacts will remain in isolation for 21 days and will be released if they test negative for the virus.

Uganda reported 20 cases and two deaths earlier in the year, but was declared Ebola-free in August.

The current outbreak, which is the DRC’s 17th, has spread rapidly since it was officially declared on May 15.

The outbreak has claimed more than 4,000 lives, according to figures released by the government on Friday, and confirmed cases have ⁠⁠reached 8,300 across seven provinces, making it the worst Ebola epidemic in the country’s history .

The World Health Organization has warned that the epidemic is “ far from over ” and on track to surpass the regional 2014-2016 West Africa Ebola outbreak, which killed more than 11,000 people, primarily in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone.

At the same time, the United Nations organisation has advised against imposing travel and trade restrictions on Kenya, DRC and Uganda following the Ebola-related death in Kenya.
