articles.title: In Nigeria’s oil-hit Niger Delta, women planted more than 3 million mangroves; 190 hectares of bare swamp forest came back green
articles.summary: Women who work with the Lokiaka Community Development Centre have planted more than 3 million mangrove saplings in Nigeria's Niger Delta since 2018 and
articles.body: Women who work with the Lokiaka Community Development Centre have planted more than 3 million mangrove saplings in Nigeria's Niger Delta since 2018 and restored about 190 hectares of damaged swamp forest, according to a report published by The Guardian on October 2, 2026. The work is being led by environmental campaigner Martha Agbani in Ogoniland, which is an area of Rivers State that is heavily affected by decades of oil pollution. More than 400 women have been trained in mangrove planting and environmental care through the programme.The damage began long before the plantingOgoniland sits within the Niger Delta, which is one of the world's major mangrove regions, and the area has a long history of oil production; pollution from spills, infrastructure and other activities has damaged land, waterways and vegetation. A 2011 assessment by the United Nations Environment Programme found extensive contamination across Ogoniland, with UNEP examining more than 200 locations and reporting that oil pollution had affected soil, groundwater, creeks, vegetation and other parts of the ecosystem.The organisation specifically identified serious damage to mangroves, and its assessment said that oil-related contamination and physical disturbance had affected mangrove vegetation, fisheries and other components of the ecosystem. UNEP recommended large-scale restoration, but also noted that continued sources of contamination had to be addressed for rehabilitation work to succeed. The loss of mangroves was not only an environmental problem for communities that live around the creeks, as fishing, harvesting and other local livelihoods depend on healthy wetlands. Agbani grew up in Ogoniland and founded the Lokiaka Community Development Centre, which works with Indigenous women and communities. The organisation initially focused on women's rights and environmental advocacy before developing its mangrove restoration work.Women became the plantersThe restoration programme trains women to collect and raise mangrove propagules and plant them in degraded wetlands. The planting is not identical at every site, as some areas are suitable for direct planting, while others require seedlings to be raised in nurseries before being moved into the swamp. Invasive nipa palms also have to be removed from some restoration sites. A 2025 report by Mongabay found that Lokiaka had trained about 300 women across four Ogoni communities and had planted 2.6 million mangrove trees since restoration began in 2018. The organisation was working in Bodo Creek, Yaataa and Teenama, where pollution and other pressures had reduced mangrove cover.Planting sites can be difficult to reach, while fishing, mining, invasive plants and other activity can interfere with newly planted trees, and Lokiaka has adjusted its methods based on conditions at individual sites rather than using one planting system everywhere. The latest Guardian report puts the cumulative total at more than 3 million mangroves and about 190 hectares of restored swamp forest, and also says that more than 400 women have been trained through the work. The restoration has taken place gradually, and teams return to sites to maintain young trees and deal with competing vegetation rather than clearing a large area and planting it once. The work also depends on local knowledge of tides, mudflats and the conditions that different mangrove species can tolerate.The forest is returning in some areasThe Guardian reported that fish and crabs have returned to some locations where they had become less common. UNEP's assessment described Ogoniland's environmental damage as extensive, and its recommendations said that mangrove restoration could take decades. The organisation also stressed the fact that restoration cannot be separated from the need to stop ongoing contamination. The scale of the restoration by Lokiaka is nevertheless significant at the community level, since more than three million mangroves have been planted since 2018, and the restored area now covers roughly 190 hectares.The programme is also tied to livelihoods for the women involved, as pollution had damaged fishing and farming opportunities in communities where women traditionally depended on natural resources. Training in nursery management and restoration has created another form of environmental work and puts women directly into decisions about damaged land. The planting continues, and Lokiaka has set a larger target of restoring millions more mangroves across the Niger Delta, while its teams continue working in individual communities where oil pollution, invasive plants and other pressures have reduced mangrove cover.More than 3 million mangroves have been planted and about 190 hectares of swamp forest have been restored since the programme began in 2018. The wider environmental recovery of Ogoniland remains a much larger project, with UNEP's assessment showing why restoration there is expected to take years rather than a single planting season.You use AI every day. articles.title: Finland orders halt to work on two Google data centres
articles.summary: The order affecting two planned data centres follows concerns over forest clearance.
articles.body:
Finnish authorities have ordered a halt to building work at two planned Google data centres amid concerns over the clearance of more than 300 hectares of forest.

The sites form part of Google's record €13bn (£11bn; $15bn) investment in Finland, announced less than a month ago and described by the company as its largest single investment in Europe.

The Finnish Supervisory Agency (LVV) said work at one site was carried out without a mandatory environmental impact assessment and ordered measures that would "significantly alter the environment" to be suspended by 23 October.

Google said it had "fallen short of our own high standards in this instance" and would follow the agency's guidance.

The orders relate to preparatory work carried out at the planned data centre sites in Muhos and Kajaani.

According to LVV's head of environment Tommi Muilu, work at the sites included the removal of trees and topsoil, the construction of site roads and storage areas, and changes to ditches.

Tuike Finland, the company behind Google's data centre projects, has been asked to provide an explanation and set out how it intends to proceed by 14 October. The agency said it could begin "enforcement proceedings" if the company failed to comply with its demand.

Hanna Halmeenpaa, chair of the Finnish Association for Nature Conservation, had previously told the AFP news agency that "nature sites which should be preserved" had been felled. The conservation group had previously called for work to be halted while the environmental requirements were examined.

In a statement to the BBC, Google said: "We understand the concerns and have fallen short of our own high standards in this instance."

It said it had "acted in good faith under the Forestry Act", carried out nature surveys and put measures in place to protect areas of high environmental value.

"As we continue our long-term work in the region, we are advancing our landscaping and biodiversity plans, which include tree planting across 130 hectares at Muhos," the company added.

Google announced last month that it would invest at least €13bn (£11bn; $15bn) in Finland over 2027 and 2028. Its plans included new data centres in Kajaani, Muhos and Vaala, alongside investment in its existing facility in Hamina.

The company said the infrastructure would help it meet growing demand for services including Search, Maps and its AI assistant Gemini.

Google said the construction phase in 2027 and 2028 would support more than 37,000 jobs and contribute an average of €3.6bn a year to Finland's economy.

As part of its expansion, Google also signed a 22-year power purchasing agreement with Finnish energy company Fortum covering up to half the capacity of the Loviisa nuclear power plant. Fortum said the agreement would help support the plant's continued operation until 2050.

Finland has attracted growing interest in data centres, with its cool climate and low-carbon electricity among the factors making it attractive to developers. Lower temperatures can also reduce the energy required to cool facilities filled with computer servers.

articles.title: Checklists, masks and mystery: What we know about the plague scare in Russia
articles.summary: Russian authorities have sought to allay global worries over the death of a young woman who worked at a Siberian anti-plague laboratory. But moves to isolate her contacts and introduce new disease-control measures at local hospitals have raised concerns among people who fear they’re not being told the full story.
articles.body: Russian authorities have sought to allay global worries over the death of a young woman who worked at a Siberian anti-plague laboratory. But moves to isolate her contacts and introduce new disease-control measures at local hospitals have raised concerns among people who fear they’re not being told the full story. The woman was a lab technician at Irkutsk Research Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia in Russia’s southeast. Questions have swirled around what illness she contracted and why Russian authorities have rushed to isolate her contacts, while downplaying the suggestion that she died of plague. CNN has learned that a local maternity hospital is subjecting patients to comprehensive health checks and requiring them to fill out questionnaires about suspicious symptoms related to “plague” and other infectious diseases. Ulyana Gavryunina, a 29-year-old blogger from Angarsk, a city in the Irkutsk region, told CNN she had to change maternity hospitals at 40 weeks pregnant after newly imposed quarantine restrictions meant her husband could no longer be with her during labor. When she arrived for a scheduled appointment at the Irkutsk City Perinatal Center, her mother, who usually accompanied her during visits, was refused entry. Staff checked her temperature, asked her to show her tongue and instructed her to wear a mask, sanitize her hands and complete two questionnaires. One of them was titled “Checklist for Suspected Highly Dangerous Infectious Disease Plague” and listed symptoms such as high fever and chest pain. Staff did not mention plague, she said, telling her only that there was an unidentified “new virus” and that extra precautions were needed to protect the babies. Inside the hospital, the atmosphere was calm, Gavryunina said. “Everything was as usual,” she told CNN. “Everyone was wearing masks, that’s all.” Her biggest concern was being told her husband could no longer accompany her during labor, even if he underwent additional medical tests. For other residents, the hospital restrictions have fueled questions about whether authorities are being transparent. “It feels like they’re not telling us the whole story,” one person who self-identified as an Irkutsk resident commented beneath one of Gavryunina’s social media posts. “They’re telling everyone that it wasn’t the plague but pneumonia. Yet hospitals are still under quarantine, and ambulance doctors are driving around in full Covid protective suits.” Another local resident, who identified herself only as Ekaterina, said life there was continuing as normal. She told CNN that while some of her acquaintances were “slightly panicking,” she had seen little change on the streets. “Everything is as usual, no visible changes,” Ekaterina said. But in local Telegram groups, many expressed skepticism. “Who are you telling these fairy tales to?” one user asked. What prompted these measures? A lab worker, identified as 28-year-old Darya Shipilova, was hospitalized on September 29, according to independent regional news outlet Lyudi Baikala. She is believed to have died at a hospital in Shelekhov, a town about 12 miles southwest of Irkutsk, at the end of last week. A friend of hers told CNN she died on October 2. The friend didn’t confirm any other details. Unverified reports suggest she fell ill after a potential lab-leak or contracted the illness after traveling to another region. Russia’s health and consumer watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, said she died of a pneumonia of “unknown” origin. The agency downplayed suspicions that her illness was related to her work. So how did the plague scare originate? The first sign of a potential issue came on October 2, when Irkutsk Governor Igor Kobzev posted on Telegram that Anna Popova, the head of Rospotrebnadzor, had convened an “extraordinary meeting” about a suspected case of a “particularly dangerous infection” in a resident of the region. Kobzev did not mention plague, but Alexey Tsydenov, the head of neighboring Buryatia, raised that possibility when he said in a statement that the woman “died of plague in the Irkutsk region.” According to Russian media reports, his statement was later edited to say that she had “possibly died from plague.” We don’t know what the lab worker was suffering from, or how she contracted her illness, but the opaque Russian response has fueled speculation. How have Russian authorities responded? Russia’s health watchdog has reassured locals that the “epidemiological situation” is stable, but local media reported that 60 workers in the Irkutsk Research Anti-Plague Institute were in quarantine and a that number of hospitals were subject to restrictions The Kremlin has urged people to rely on updates from the health watchdog rather than “various rumors and speculation.” When pressed for further information on Tuesday, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov again referred journalists to the health watchdog, noting it “continues its work.” But the watchdog has released limited information. What has been the international response? US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday urged Russia to share more information about the circumstances of the researcher’s death. “I think it’s incumbent upon Russia to obviously share more information with the world,” he said. “Maybe it’s bigger than we thought. We don’t know, but I think it would be reckless at this moment, given the limited information we still have, to speculate.” The World Health Organization said it was in contact with Russian health authorities to “verify the event, its circumstances, the laboratory tests underway, and their results.” “Based on unofficial information available, the public health risk to the general population appears to be low,” it said. Despite such reassurances, several countries in the region have said they are monitoring and have put safeguard measures in place. Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan and Tajikistan have implemented quarantine controls at state border crossing points. Uzbekistan said it has “increased the readiness” of authorities to deal with highly infectious diseases. Why was the lab studying the plague? According to its website, the Anti-Plague Institute employs around 95 researchers and is a major public health facility responsible for monitoring and preventing outbreaks of high-risk bacterial and viral infections across Siberia and Russia’s Far East. The institute was established in 1934 to combat plague and continues to study the disease because Yersinia pestis, the bacterium that causes the plague, still circulates naturally in wildlife across parts of Siberia and neighboring regions.

articles.title: Amid turbulence in US-India ties, American lawmakers honor pilot's courage
articles.summary: The TOI correspondent from Washington: In a rare gesture of congressional recognition for an Indian national, a bipartisan group of U.S.
articles.body: The TOI correspondent from Washington: In a rare gesture of congressional recognition for an Indian national, a bipartisan group of U.S. lawmakers has introduced a resolution honoring Captain Smit Machchhar, the Indian pilot who helped prevent a suicidal terrorist attack aboard a Flydubai flight bound for Israel last week.The resolution, introduced Monday by New Jersey Democrat Josh Gottheimer, with Republican Reps Michael McCaul of Texas and Don Bacon of Nebraska as cosponsors, praises Machchhar for what it calls “extraordinary courage in protecting every soul aboard his aircraft.”The honor comes even as relations between Washington and New Delhi have entered one of their more difficult periods in the Trump era, with disagreements over tariffs, India's purchase of Russian oil and wider geopolitical differences complicating what had been a steadily deepening strategic partnership. U.S.-India trade negotiations have again stalled, with Washington retaining the possibility of significantly higher tariffs on Indian goods, and there has been a sharp uptick in anti-Indian xenophobia on social media platforms in the U.S.Machchhar's heroism, meanwhile, has provided a point of uncomplicated convergence among India, the U.S and Israel. According to the congressional resolution, the House should “commend the heroic actions of the off-duty pilots, cabin crew, and passengers who secured the flight deck and brought the aircraft safely down” and condemn the attack as “an act of terrorism and as an attack on the safety of international civil aviation.” It also calls for a full investigation by Saudi Arabia and the UAE.For Gottheimer, the resolution fits neatly into a congressional career built around national security, Israel and bipartisan cooperation. A fifth-term Democrat, he is the ranking member of the National Security Agency and Cyber Subcommittee on the House Intelligence Committee. He is also a member of the Congressional Caucus on India and Indian-Americans who worked as a speechwriter in the Clinton White House before moving through the private sector and eventually to Congress.Machchhar’s heroism is also an unlikely but powerful bridge at a moment when the broader India-U.S. relationship is being tested by the transactional politics of the MAGA era. While governments argue over tariffs and Russian oil, the U.S Congress is sending a different message: whatever the disputes between Washington and New Delhi, an Indian professional who risked his life to save Americans, Israelis and other passengers can still command bipartisan American admiration.You use AI every day. articles.title: Tuareg rebels withdraw from strategic town of Kidal in northern Mali
articles.summary: The Azawad Liberation Front said sustained air strikes by Malian troops and Russian allies forced its tactical retreat.
articles.body:
Mali’s Tuareg rebels have announced they are withdrawing from the strategic town of Kidal, in the north of the country.

The Azawad Liberation Front (FLA), a coalition formed in 2024 uniting Tuareg and northern separatist factions, said in a statement on Tuesday that it had decided to carry out a “controlled withdrawal” from Kidal six months after capturing the town and amid fresh air strikes by Mali’s military backed by Russian fighters.

“The FLA specifies that this is a temporary operational measure, also intended to preserve its human and logistical capabilities intact. This methodical withdrawal from the area took place without any direct combat having yet pitted its forces against the enemy,” the statement said.

Earlier on Tuesday, Mali’s military said it had launched large-scale air and ground operations in the region ⁠⁠around Kidal.

The goals of the operations included “tracking down and neutralizing” armed groups ⁠⁠in the area, destroying their supply networks, and restoring “lasting security” and free movement for people and goods, a Malian military statement said.

Pro-government fighters, including Russian paramilitaries, re-entered Kidal on Tuesday afternoon, a security source said.

Mali has been gripped by conflict since 2012, when a Tuareg separatist rebellion in the north was overtaken by al-Qaeda-linked Islamist militants, who later consolidated under Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM) in 2017.

While the FLA presents itself as a secular nationalist movement seeking independence for Mali’s Azawad region and JNIM is an al-Qaeda-affiliated group, the two sides have set ideological differences aside to confront the Malian government.

The FLA says it remains committed to independence for Azawad, the name separatists use for northern Mali, while JNIM says it is fighting to “liberate” Mali and overthrow the government.

The military has ruled the country since a 2021 coup, pledging to restore order and unity.

JNIM has gained in strength ‌‌since the Malian soldiers who seized power expelled French forces and some 15,000 United Nations peacekeepers, ‌‌and turned to Russian paramilitaries for defence support.

Since the FLA and JNIM launched a joint offensive in April, the conflict has escalated with increasing attacks on the military-backed government forces.

The Malian government says it is working to restore state authority and dismantle what it calls a “terrorist alliance” between the FLA and JNIM.

articles.title: In 2018, Dutch engineers replaced a bike path with hollow panels made from recycled plastic; after 1 million crossings, the trial reported 50–70% lower carbon emissions, and rain storage reached 48% capacity
articles.summary: Discover how Dutch engineers have transformed bike paths using hollow panels made from recycled plastic, achieving 50-70% lower carbon emissions and innovative stormwater management after 1 million rides.
articles.body: From above, a bicycle path typically appears straightforward, with a strip of ground underneath it, a hard surface, and painted markings. By substituting hollow prefabricated panels made mostly of recycled plastic for a traditional route, engineers in the Netherlands used that hidden area as part of the experiment. Three concepts were combined to create the Plastic Road prototype. The panels' hollow innards might temporarily store stormwater, their modular design could make parts easier to install or repair, and they could provide used plastic a second chance at life.The first pilot, a 30-metre path in Zwolle, opened in September 2018, followed by a second in Giethoorn that November Wavin/Orbia release. By May 2020, the Zwolle path had registered its millionth bicycle crossing. The project team also estimated that the pilot design produced around 50% to 70% lower carbon emissions than typical asphalt or concrete-tile bike lanes. The initiative was an experiment, not a suggestion that plastic roads should replace conventional pavement everywhere. But the never-ending flow of bicycle traffic and the constant monitoring by sensors gave engineers more data than a short laboratory trial could deliver.The hollow space under the pathThe Plastic Road was not a slab of plastic simply laid on the ground. It used prefabricated modular parts with a hollow space below the surface. That hollow space had several purposes. In a heavy rainstorm, it could give space for rainfall, and the same design could also fit wires, pipelines and sensors without having to dig up the pavement later. The Province of Overijssel's 2018 annual report describes the Zwolle section as made of recycled plastic and fitted with sensors for continuous monitoring. It calls the construction a climate-adaptive system, because the internal space can temporarily hold rainfall. The pilot was never meant to represent a whole citywide cycle network, since the Zwolle section was only about 30 metres long.A million bicycle crossingsThe first path in Zwolle opened in September 2018, and the second pilot followed in Giethoorn that November. Sensors in the sections tracked temperature, bicycle passes and loading, allowing the developers to observe how the modular structure behaved rather than relying on visual inspections alone. In May 2020 the project recorded its one millionth bicycle crossing. Developers said the paths had withstood everyday bicycle traffic as well as heavier loads such as maintenance vehicles and garbage trucks after more than a year and a half of testing.The one-million figure is useful because it represents repeated real-world loading. It does not mean the path experienced one million identical stress events, nor does it establish a lifespan of one million rides. It simply shows that the pilot had accumulated a substantial amount of use before the developers moved toward commercialization. A product can perform well during a limited test while still requiring much longer monitoring before engineers can establish how it behaves over decades.Where the carbon figure comes fromThe carbon claim needs similar context. The 50% to 70% estimate compared the pilot design with typical bicycle lanes built of asphalt or concrete slabs, and it relates to the pilot's production and construction processes, not to all possible roads made of recycled plastic. Factors such as the source of recycled plastic, manufacturing energy, transport, and the comparison pavement influence life-cycle calculations.Subsequent work on the technology needed a separate environmental review. An independent life cycle assessment of the later Plastic Road CCL series showed fewer carbon emissions than several reference pavement options; however, the numbers were based on the later product rather than just replicating the original 2018 pilot study. That is why the 50% to 70% figure applies only to the 2018 pilot and should not be read as a general property of plastic pavement.Where the rainwater wentThe hollow structure also provided space for stormwater, so not every heavy rain had to go straight to the normal drainage. Sensors showed that the highest water level in the Zwolle structure reached only 48% of its storage capacity during heavy showers, and the water infiltrated into the soil within two days, according to Wavin.This is a relevant finding for Dutch towns, where so much concrete can make it difficult for rainfall to penetrate the earth straight away. A structure that provides temporary storage just below the path can reduce the amount of water traditional drainage must handle at any one time. Research on modular plastic pavement has also highlighted this internal volume as one of the main differences between prefabricated hollow plastic systems and regular roadways. A 2023 study examining prefabricated plastic pavement systems described hollow modules as a way to combine a lightweight road structure with space for utilities and temporary water storage.What the experiment provedThe Dutch Plastic Road did not prove that all bike paths have to be recycled plastic. Its pilots were short, the design was still evolving and the carbon figure was the developers' own estimate, while the crossing count and the 48% water level came from sensor monitoring. After the pilots, the team formed a standalone company, PlasticRoad, in 2020 to prepare for commercial production. In this pilot, the notable idea was the combination of repurposed material, modular construction and hidden water storage.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Tear gas in Paris and Marseille as school protests spread and grow across France
articles.summary: Crowds of mainly teenagers called for more resources for schools and an end to what they called police repression.
articles.body:
Hundreds of thousands of people have taken to the streets across France, as a wave of protests by high-school pupils spread to their parents, university students and unions.

Crowds of teenagers marched from the Place de la République in Paris, calling for more resources for schools, and what they called less repression from police.

Police clashed with demonstrators in Lyon, used tear gas in Paris and Marseille and water cannon in Rennes, but there was little of the serious trouble that marred previous protests.

Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu condemned the earlier violence and said since the protests had begun 215 students and 85 staff had been hurt as well as 715 police officers.

The government said there had been disruption in 891 high schools on Tuesday - almost a quarter of all lycées - and said more than 250,000 demonstrators had taken to the streets during the day.

Students' unions put the number at 450,000, and said the number of high schools blockaded was 1,800 on what the protesters dubbed "Act Three" of their movement.

In Marseille, thousands of demonstrators moved around this city, stopping momentarily to chant before moving on as police changed direction.

A group of masked protesters grabbed bollards and bins and tried to barricade themselves off from police. Riot officers fired tear gas, and the protesters dispersed.

"Most of us aren't violent," said Alissa, a student in Marseille. "We're going to the streets because they've closed our schools... schools are falling apart."

Her friend, Sacha, said the ceilings in Marseille's schools were leaking and conditions were generally rather poor, "so we can't really work a lot of time". "We will keep doing this until good measures are taken," he added.

In parliament, the prime minister accused the radical-left France Unbowed (LFI) party of seeking to "sow chaos" ahead of presidential elections in seven months' time.

President Emmanuel Macron is nearing the end of his second and final term in office and LFI leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon is currently runner-up in the opinion polls behind Marine Le Pen of the hard-right National Rally.

Macron was due to chair a meeting with ministers at the Élysée Palace on Tuesday evening to assess the situation.

Education Minister Édouard Geffray said that from the start he had appealed for dialogue rather than school blockades and complained that "ultra-violent elements infiltrated the high-school student movements".

He is now under pressure to respond to the students' demands. What has been offered, including a website for students to express their grievances and an afternoon of internal discussion in schools on Friday, has made little impression so far.

There seems little chance of the protests coming to an end just yet. France's biggest union, the CGT, has said that further protests involving school and university students are being planned for Thursday.

There is widespread concern over allegations of "disproportionate force" by police, and France's IGPN police inspectorate has been investigating a number of cases.

One police officer who fired a tear-gas grenade at a high school student at Saint-Ouen-l'Aumône, north-west of Paris, last week has now been charged by prosecutors with "violence... resulting in mutilation or permanent disability".

Eden, 14, was part of a group blockading the Château d'Épluches lycée for 15-18-year-olds when he was hit in the face. His lawyer said he suffered a fractured jaw, and that his upper teeth were broken and four of his lower teeth were gone.

On Monday, a 15-year-old's hand was torn off after a so-called anti-encirclement grenade was fired in unclear circumstances near a school in the northern city of Lens.

Authorities say he picked up the "sting ball" grenade which then exploded, but students allege he was hit directly after an officer fired.

The grenade is considered a non-lethal weapon and the local prefect has said the incident took place when police were confronted by a group of 200-250 students throwing stones and fireworks.

Teenager's hand blown off during confrontation between France school protesters and police

School protests send shivers down French government's spine

What began with local anger at overcrowded classrooms, a lack of teaching staff and dilapidated school buildings in the northern Paris suburb of Seine-Saint-Denis in mid-September has since spread across the country, and extended to some universities too.

Late on Tuesday, the French interior ministry said a total of 6,547 had been stopped or arrested by police since 28 September.

Tuesday's protests drew people of all ages. One couple in their 70s, Alain and Michèle, joined the march in central Paris, to show their support for young students, explaining that as former teachers they understood the problems that France's education system was facing.

"We are the grandparents of three students who are all mobilised. They have protested peacefully in front of their respective high schools in Paris in recent days, but they were still tear-gassed," Alain told the BBC, his voice trembling.

Additional reporting by Manon Prat in Paris.

articles.title: Amid protests, Kosovo’s political deadlock raises prospect of new elections
articles.summary: Kosovo faces tensions as protests against former rebel leaders’ convictions coincide with the prospect of new elections.
articles.body:
Kosovo faces the risk of turmoil as protests against the convictions of former Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) leaders coincide with a midnight deadline to elect a president.

Demonstrators have called for changes to the law governing the Hague-based Kosovo Specialist Chambers, including measures affecting prison terms and where sentences are served. The protests follow the September 16 convictions of former KLA leaders, including former President Hashim Thaci.

The protesters’ demands have become entangled with negotiations over the presidency, raising the prospect of new elections if lawmakers fail to reach an agreement by Wednesday. November 15 has emerged as a likely date for a new vote.

“New elections do not, in themselves, promise anything particularly positive,” political analyst Artan Muhaxhiri told Al Jazeera. “The chances of a radical political change are slim.”

He said that if a president is not elected, a new vote will take place in a tense political climate.

Anger over the verdicts will become a central campaign issue, he said, “overshadowing fundamental questions of socioeconomic development, and deepening the country’s downward spiral of systemic instability”.

In 2015, the Specialist Chambers were established under Kosovo law following international investigations into alleged war crimes committed by KLA members during and after the 1998-99 conflict. Although formally part of Kosovo’s judicial system, the court sits in The Hague. But it remains contentious in Kosovo because the KLA is widely revered for having fought against Serbian rule.

In September, protests erupted after the court sentenced Thaci to 25 years in prison.

Later, the opposition Democratic Party of Kosovo (PDK) – formerly led by Thaci – proposed amendments aimed at curbing the tribunal. The plan included capping prison sentences at 15 years, allowing convicts to serve their sentences in Kosovo, enabling appeals before Kosovo’s Supreme Court, granting presidential pardons and narrowing the court’s temporal jurisdiction.

On October 2, 2026, Prime Minister Albin Kurti’s government concluded that there were no legal obstacles to the PDK initiative and forwarded its assessment to the parliament, the Assembly of Kosovo. Days later, Kosovo’s parliament approved the initiative at first reading, although it has not been finally adopted.

Meanwhile, Kosovo has been mired in a political impasse after the expiration of President Vjosa Osmani’s term in April, as the National Assembly has been unable to select a new president.

Now, internal power struggles within the PDK following the September sentencing have left the party fragmented, rendering the largest opposition party incapable of negotiating a cross-party presidential compromise, according to Nexhmedin Spahiu, a Pristina-based professor of political science.

On Monday, as lawmakers failed to secure a quorum to elect a president, police deployed tear gas and water cannon outside the Assembly, following clashes involving fireworks and bottles. The use of force prompted criticism from observers.

Pristina-based journalist Gezim Baxhaku believes special police units overstepped their legal authority.

“There was an overuse of force,” Baxhaku told Al Jazeera. He said that while protesters threw firecrackers, police “exceeded their legal powers and acted entirely contrary to the situation on the ground”.

Among the hundreds of protesters were KLA veterans.

Pristina had witnessed nearly three weeks of largely peaceful gatherings before Monday’s escalation.

“Citizens were routinely bringing food, water, and coffee to the officers on duty,” Baxhaku said. “There was absolutely no reason for this to happen. For the first time since the late 2000s, police acted in such an uncalled-for manner – reacting upon orders to escalate a situation.”

Spahiu, the political science professor, said the protests should not be understood as a sign that people in Kosovo broadly reject the verdicts.

“A large majority of citizens in Kosovo are satisfied with the decision of the Specialist Chambers in The Hague,” said Spahiu.

He told Al Jazeera that the court’s rejection of Serbian claims of systematic crimes against humanity by the KLA “validated the liberation struggle”.

“Furthermore, people are relieved that individuals are finally being held accountable for crimes committed against political rivals within the Albanian community itself,” he said.

The political deadlock and Kurti’s ‘transactional’ approach

The Assembly remains deadlocked over the election of a head of state, as the PDK and other opposition parties boycott the voting session, denying the legislature its constitutionally required 80-MP quorum.

Muhaxhiri blamed Kurti for the crisis, criticising his decision to link the presidential vote to the Hague court amendments.

“Tensions escalated further when Kurti presented a plan based on a transactional approach to two fundamentally distinct issues: linking the draft law amending the Law on the Specialist Chambers to the election of the new president,” said Muhaxhiri.

“In effect, this amounted to a quid pro quo. By doing so, he appeared to be placing the historical, national, and identity-related significance of the liberation war on the same political bargaining table as the immediate objective of electing a president who would serve his political interests.”

images.caption: A Kosovo police officer kicks a flare near the parliament building during the extraordinary session to vote limiting the powers of the Hague-based war crimes court, weeks after it sentenced former President Hashim Thaci and other Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) [Valdrin Xhemaj/Reuters]

articles.title: Catalan separatist Puigdemont to return to Spain after warrant lifted
articles.summary: Spain’s Constitutional Court ruled an amnesty law for Catalan separatists applied to the politician.
articles.body:
Self-exiled Catalan separatist leader Carles Puigdemont could be set to return to Spain after the country’s Constitutional Court ruled that an amnesty law for Catalan separatists applies to embezzlement charges against Puigdemont.

A Supreme Court judge then lifted a warrant for Puigdemont’s arrest on Tuesday, clearing the way for his return without fear of arrest.

Puigdemont, then president of Catalonia, fled to Belgium in 2017 after holding an independence referendum for his self-governing region to break away from Spain. Madrid said the vote was illegal.

Catalonia unilaterally declared independence from Spain that year after the referendum, with 90 percent of voters backing independence.

He has since avoided several extradition attempts by Spain to face trial over the vote, while many of his confidants and supporters spent time in prison.

Members of Puigdemont’s political party Junts welcomed his potential return.

“It’s a great victory for President Puigdemont and the two other exiled ‌[leaders in Belgium]”, Jordi Turull, secretary-general of Junts, told reporters.

“They held firm, they resisted, they prevailed in Europe, and today they have prevailed against the Spanish state.”

Puigdemont appears set to return to Spain just as the country is preparing for a snap election in November, although an official from his Junts party said he is unlikely to take part.

Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez was only able to remain in power in 2023 when Puigdemont’s Junts party, along with another Catalan party, backed his new government in exchange for the amnesties.

A year ago, Junts withdrew its support for the minority central government, and the party was decisive in Spain’s progressive government losing two key votes in parliament this week when it tried to push through emergency housing measures amid street protests .

Sanchez responded by calling a November snap election, hoping anger over housing will mobilise his voters.

The prime minister told ⁠reporters on Tuesday he did not regret launching the amnesty and welcomed the court ruling.

“I believe the important message is that of coexistence among Catalans,” he said.

Although separatism has lost ground and Junts is trailing in opinion polls, Puigdemont’s return could prompt renewed political drama.

Spain’s conservative People’s Party is leading in opinion polls ahead ‌of the election and may need to seek the support of Junts and other centre-right parties to govern.

articles.title: Three arrested after raid on gang accused of helping migrants pretend to be gay to get asylum
articles.summary: Those targeted by Home Office immigration enforcement officers are accused of charging migrants up to £4,500 for fabricated evidence.
articles.body:
Immigration enforcement have made arrests in connection with a suspected criminal network believed to be behind dozens of fake asylum claims from people pretending to be gay.

It follows a BBC investigation earlier this year , which revealed that law firms and advisers were helping migrants pose as gay in an effort to get asylum.

Those targeted by Home Office immigration enforcement officers this morning are accused of charging migrants up to £4,500 for fabricated evidence, including staged photographs and fake documents.

They are thought to have aided dozens of asylum claims from Bangladeshi men, claiming they would be in fear for their lives if they returned home.

Two people were arrested at addresses in London this morning on suspicion of fraud and immigration offences, with Home Office officers also seizing phones, jewellery and thousands of pounds in cash. A third person was arrested on suspicion of being in the country illegally.

Chris Foster, a regional lead for criminal investigations at the Home Office, said the fake claims were connected to a Bangladeshi community LGBT organisation called Apanjon, which is based in Whitechapel, east London.

He said asylum caseworkers had initially spotted patterns in suspicious claims, which raised concerns about the group, and that immigration officers had been investigating for several months.

"We've got some intelligence that they can provide fake letters and documents, and they could charge anywhere between £1,000 and £4,500," Foster said.

"It could be letters of support from Apanjon, it could be staged photographs, suggesting that these people are gay, it could be letters from people claiming to be in a friendship or a sexual relationship - [a] same-sex relationship - as the claimants."

More than 100 asylum claims linked to the criminal network are being reviewed by the Home Office. Foster said some of the fake asylum applications would have "undoubtedly" been granted.

Immigration judges have previously criticised evidence from Apanjon as unreliable or not credible and found that an applicant who claimed to have attended the group's events had submitted staged photographs.

The Home Office said the group would often vouch for men who claimed asylum on the basis they were gay only after having initially been refused on political grounds. In one case, a man didn't raise his sexuality until nine years after his original claim.

The group is accused of using the same tactics as those pushed by advisers exposed in the BBC's investigation earlier this year.

A Home Office spokesperson said it was continuing to review asylum claims linked to that reporting, which led to two arrests in May.

In the BBC report, published in April, an adviser called Tanisa Khan told an undercover reporter she could provide a "comprehensive package", including photographs at gay clubs and other supporting evidence.

She was linked to a community group called Worcester LGBT, which she told the reporter they should attend in order to add to evidence for his fake claim.

Men attending one of the group's events at a community centre in Beckton, east London, claimed they were not really gay. One said: "Nobody is a gay here. Not even 1% are gay. Not even 0.01% are gay."

The investigation also revealed how bogus medical conditions and fake news websites were being used to bolster fraudulent asylum claims.

Worcester LGBT has since closed. Its founder previously said the group did not create or support fabricated evidence in asylum claims and it was not up to the organisation to determine whether any individual was actually gay.

Khan blamed communication difficulties for a "misunderstanding" and denied advising the reporter to make a false claim or offering to create fabricated evidence.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said "those faking persecution are beneath contempt and mock real victims who need protection".

"To the gangs profiting from this disgraceful fraud: you will be prosecuted, stripped of your dirty money and shut down," she said.

"And to those cheating the system, your claim will be thrown out, and you will be removed from this country."

A conviction for asylum fraud carries a maximum sentence of up to 10 years in prison.

articles.title: Russia denies imposing anti-plague measures after lab worker death
articles.summary: Russia denies plague cases after laboratory technician’s death; US demands ‘transparency’ as WHO monitors situation.
articles.body:
Russian authorities have denied that they imposed anti-plague measures after a laboratory technician died of suspected pneumonic plague in a case which has drawn international scrutiny.

Russian media reported that a 28-year-old woman named Darya Shipilova , who had been working at the Irkutsk Anti-plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East, died from suspected pneumonic plague on Friday.

Rospotrebnadzor, Russia’s health watchdog, said on Tuesday that no cases of plague had been detected among staff who had come ⁠into contact with the laboratory worker for the past 10 days.

“This included identifying the widest possible circle of individuals who had been in contact with the patient and arranging for them to be placed under medical observation in hospital with daily laboratory tests,” the watchdog said.

The institute said in a statement that extensive testing during an autopsy on the woman’s body found no microorganisms linked to her work at the anti-plague institute.

It said results had revealed two cases of COVID-19 and two cases of rhinovirus infection, but that no pathogens causing other infectious diseases had been detected.

Elena Sofina, deputy head of the Shelekhov district near Irkutsk, where a local hospital was placed under quarantine, said no “dangerous diagnosis” had been confirmed.

She added that 60 percent of ⁠those placed under quarantine as a precaution had already been released.

Local media said about 200 people ⁠had previously been quarantined.

US Secretary ⁠of State Marco Rubio said on Tuesday it was incumbent on Moscow to share more information on Friday.

“Anytime you hear there is a disease that infected someone in a lab anywhere in the world, you’re going to be concerned about it, especially given recent events not so long ago in 2020 and 2021 when we saw that happen. That said, it would be irresponsible for me to sit here and speculate,” Rubio said.

The World Health Organization in Geneva said on Tuesday that Russia had told it there were no ⁠cases of plague in the city of Irkutsk.

It was unclear if this meant that the laboratory technician’s death was unrelated to plague infection.

Plague is a bacterial disease that can occur in several forms, including pneumonic plague, which is the most contagious type and can be transmitted by respiratory means. Bubonic plague is transmitted by infected fleas.

Pneumonic plague, which causes lung failure, can be fatal if not treated early, according to the WHO.

articles.title: South Korea’s Lee says AI appears to have been used in bank hacks
articles.summary: South Korean President Lee Jae Myung said on Tuesday that AI models are believed to have been used in some recent hacking incidents against banks and called for the country to develop cybersecurity methods suited to the AI era.
articles.body: South Korean President Lee Jae Myung said on Tuesday that AI models are believed to have been used in some recent hacking incidents against banks and called for the country to develop cybersecurity methods suited to the AI era. “In some hacking incidents, signs have emerged of AI being used, causing considerable public concern and anxiety,” Lee said during a cabinet meeting. “Please establish the circumstances swiftly and clearly, and concentrate personnel and resources on minimizing the damage.” South Korea‘s police have launched a full-scale investigation into the hacking attacks against commercial banks that led to a breach of customers’ personal information, the Yonhap news agency reported on Tuesday. Shinhan Bank, KB Kookmin Bank and others had reported cyberattacks, the Financial Services Commission (FSC) said on Friday, while Yonhap reported that Hana Bank and Woori Bank also suffered breaches. Authorities have not yet disclosed details on what kind of AI tools were used in the hacking incidents or the full scale of the breaches. On Sunday, FSC Chairman Lee Eog-weon convened an emergency meeting with financial industry associations, regulators and executives from affected institutions, warning that the sector must respond with the highest level of vigilance. Financial watchdog the Financial Supervisory Service (FSS) and the Financial Security Institute shared data about 28 unique IP addresses and some country information linked to the recent hacking attempts with the financial sector, the FSS said on Tuesday. In September, Australia said an OpenAI agent breached a government health data portal in June, gaining unauthorized access to files, in what could be the ‌first known instance of an AI agent hacking a government website. An artificial intelligence research firm said last week that AI agents tried to hack into a Canadian government website, casting the effort as a failed hacking attempt, while Canada said there were ​no indications its systems were compromised.

images.caption: South Korean President Lee Jae-myung during a news conference at the presidential office in Seoul on June 4, 2025. Lee began his five-year term without a transition period earlier in the day as he won a snap election following the impeachment of former President Yoon Suk Yeol over his failed martial law bid in December.

articles.title: Yemen’s government is on the attack against the Houthis. What has changed?
articles.summary: Yemeni forces are trying to reverse Houthi gains, aided by heavier air power and renewed international support.
articles.body:
Yemen’s internationally recognised government wants to show that it has finally taken the initiative against the Houthis in the country’s long-running war.

The announcement of Operation Dawn of Yemen on Monday to restore state authority across the country was quickly followed by a military offensive on the southern Red Sea coast.

The initial aim is to reverse gains made by the Houthis last month, when the Iranian-backed group took control of one of the world’s most important waterways, the Bab al-Mandeb Strait . But the ultimate goal of the operation is to retake the areas of the country held by the Houthis for more than a decade, including the capital, Sanaa, which they seized by force in 2014 and later imposed their own government.

It is a lofty ambition, and the achievements so far have been modest – most notably a limited advance into areas near Bab al-Mandeb.

Still, the attacks indicate that the Saudi-backed Yemeni government operation is being conducted in a more organised manner – particularly notable after last month’s capitulation and loss of the Red Sea coast to the Houthis, also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God).

The main issues faced by government forces in early September included a lack of cohesiveness among the groups fighting against the Houthis and a lack of military preparedness, as well as what analysts have described as Houthi infiltration of government forces’ communications.

It is too early to say whether those problems have been resolved, but the inability of the Houthis to secure the highlands overlooking the areas they conquered in the southern Red Sea has left them vulnerable to a counteroffensive.

There are a number of other factors that, when taken together, suggest the government’s shift to the attack may bring about more success than it has enjoyed since fighting resumed in Yemen in July, ending a fragile truce that had been in place since 2022.

Most notable has been the involvement of Saudi Arabia, which is providing heavy aerial support. On Monday, the Saudi-led coalition supporting the Yemeni government said that 100 fighter jets had participated in the offensive, its first acknowledgment in four years – since a 2022 truce – that it had resumed air attacks against the Houthis, despite reports of strikes in September.

The air strikes have aided government forces attacking the Houthis on multiple fronts aside from the Red Sea coast, including Taiz, Marib and al-Jawf.

Maged al-Madhaji, chairman of the Sana’a Center for Strategic Studies, told Al Jazeera that the “rate and accuracy of the air strikes” was higher than it had previously been, even compared with the start of the Saudi-led coalition’s anti-Houthi bombing campaign in 2015.

Coupled with intelligence from the United States, the strikes were more efficient and coordinated with ground forces. A US official told Al Jazeera on Monday that 200 US advisers were stationed in Saudi Arabia in support of the campaign.

Elias Hanna, a retired Lebanese general, said the coordination revealed a unified command structure that was vital to military success.

“[There is] a central leadership managing operations and coordination between the ground forces and the air forces,” he told Al Jazeera on Monday. “The air force attacks, but ground forces then have to occupy the territory, remain there, and control it.”

The US expertise, Hanna added, essentially provided an “intelligence bank” of targets that would be able to repeatedly attack Houthi positions.

Another factor that has so far set the government offensive apart from the fighting in early September has been the prominent role taken by the Giants Brigades.

Previously trained by the United Arab Emirates and now backed by Saudi Arabia, the force had been present during the losses to the Houthis in the Red Sea, but in smaller numbers. This time it has been leading the battle in the area and in Taiz’s al-Waziyah district, which overlooks the port city of Mocha.

The Giants Brigades previously defeated the Houthis in Shabwah in 2022 and drove them out of the southeastern coastal governorate, as well as parts of Marib and al-Bayda east of Sanaa.

“They are the most experienced with the Houthis’ fighting methods,” said al-Madhaji, “because they are the force that has engaged them the most across different theatres of operations – some on flat terrain and some mountainous .”

“In practice, this is the first time we have seen Saudi operational management, together with forces that had been under Emirati management, produce effective results,” added al-Madhaji. “That suggests the operations room has become unified and that operational coordination between the different sides has become more effective.”

Less attention has been paid to the fighting in Marib and al-Jawf, two largely desert governorates east of Sanaa, but government forces have also claimed advances there.

Developments there could prove crucial to what the government has said is its ultimate aim: the recapture of Sanaa, held by the Houthis since 2014. Increased coordination between ground forces, air power and intelligence gathering is the only way a multi-pronged assault towards the capital could be managed, although that still appears to be distant.

The Houthis themselves cannot be discounted. Their forces have so far held firm and regrouped after the losses on Monday in the southwestern town of Dhubab on the Red Sea, and continue to advance towards the government-held city of Taiz, one of the country’s most important centres.

Morale on the government side is fragile – more setbacks, particularly in Taiz, would change the narrative once again.

The Houthis also have strong missile and drone capabilities – strengthened over the past four years – and have already increased their attacks on government forces as well as Saudi Arabia. Forcing them out of territory they have recently claimed is difficult, but forcing them out of territory they have held for years – like the major port city of Hodeidah – will be even harder.

Yet unlike in previous escalations of the conflict, the government and Saudi Arabia have stronger international backing.

The Houthis can attack Red Sea shipping to demonstrate the damage they can inflict if attacked, but that also highlights the dangers of allowing the group to retain control in the region, particularly as Iran conducts a similar policy on the other side of the Arabian Peninsula, in the Strait of Hormuz.

The United Kingdom has already said it will provide defensive support to Saudi Arabia, and on Monday the kingdom’s mutual-defence pact with Turkiye and Pakistan was also activated . Ankara has not confirmed any troop deployments, but Islamabad has said that it was involved in support roles, including “reconnaissance”.

That international support may prove vital – both diplomatically and militarily – to the success of the anti-Houthi operation, one that is likely to drag on for many months.

articles.body: A former high-ranking CIA official who embezzled nearly $200 million from the federal government lied about his military background and education to climb the ranks at the spy agency, federal prosecutors revealed. David J. Rush pleaded guilty in Virginia federal court to one count of wire fraud. His plea comes months after an FBI raid on his home uncovered 298 gold bars worth $46 million, $2.1 million in cash and dozens of luxury items. "Federal employees are entrusted with serving the American people, not themselves," said Attorney General Todd Blanche. "The Trump Administration is committed to rooting out waste, fraud, and abuse in the federal government, including by prosecuting those who foolishly defraud American taxpayers." UFO WHISTLEBLOWER CLAIMS BILLIONS IN SECRET SPENDING HIDDEN FROM CONGRESS To reach the upper echelons of the CIA and secure top-secret clearances, Rush fabricated extensive credentials. On official job applications, he claimed to be a graduate of the U.S. Air Force Test Pilot School and the director of test operations for a joint Army/Navy unit. In reality, Rush was never a pilot, held no FAA licenses, and served primarily as an information systems technician during his time in the Navy. Once positioned in senior leadership, Rush executed a massive siphon of taxpayer dollars. He created fictitious government entities and fake initiatives — including a phony "Special Access Program" — to redirect federal funds into his own accounts, ultimately stealing $194 million, according to the Justice Department. articles.title: Gia Duddy & Bengals boyfriend go to war with Instagram trolls, Brock Purdy embraces his dad-core fashion
articles.summary: Gia Duddy's Instagram comments exploded after Bengals wide receiver Andrei Iosivas confirmed their relationship while fighting with a random commenter.
articles.body: 'Nightcaps' is a daily column that catches you up on the biggest sports, news and culture stories you may have missed while pretending to do work at your desk. It runs Monday-Friday on OutKick.com. For all of you, it is Tuesday. For me, it's Friday. Because tomorrow, my happy butt is getting on a plane and flying to Myrtle Beach for a little girl's trip with one of my best friends from grad school. I am looking forward to a few days of beach-rotting, water sports, seafood and... the Mini Golf Masters. Yes, that is a thing. And I will be attending Championship Saturday. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE I have no idea what to expect. Is it like regular golf? Does everyone have to be quiet and silence their phones? Is there a dress code? Will there be green jackets? Do the professionals absolutely nail the windmill hole every single time? Rest assured, I will report back. In the meantime, let's do some Nightcaps! There's a war going on in Gia Duddy's Instagram comments You remember Gia Duddy, right? She went ultra mega viral as Will Levis' hot girlfriend during the 2023 NFL Draft — until they broke up five minutes later, Levis publicly professed his love for mayonnaise and then Gia became an influencer. There was also that video leak... but we won't go there. Anyway, now she's dating Bengals wide receiver Andrei Iosivas. And I know this because Iosivas confirmed it himself while fighting with some random dude in Gia's Instagram comments. It started when Gia posted photos from Sunday's Bengals game, and someone commented asking who her mystery man was. Another guy responded, "WR45 on the depth chart Andrei Iosivas." Which is objectively a pretty funny way to answer that question. Iosivas, however, did not find it funny. "plz get ur husband off my girls page," he responded, tagging the guy's wife. Oh, we're doing this. The guy fired back that Iosivas should "get back to running special teams coverage" and said Gia had been "passed around half the league." Gia then jumped in herself, tagged the wife AGAIN and called the guy a great role model for his daughters. From there, it just got nastier, and I'm not going to reprint the whole thing here. But I do appreciate finding out about a new relationship via an NFL wide receiver fighting for his life in his girlfriend's Instagram comments. Gia does seem to be settling nicely into her second stint as an NFL WAG, though. Well, except for one small problem. She has to live in Ohio. STAY "FEARLESS" ON THE GO! TAKE TOMI LAHREN WITH YOU. DOWNLOAD THE TLIF PODCAST NOW! Last week, Gia posted a TikTok lamenting the less glamorous side of WAG life, namely that roster moves keep taking all her friends away. One of them was apparently headed to Miami. "B****, I'm in Cincinnati, Ohio. You're going to Miami? Bring me with you," she said. Apparently eating Skyline Chili and going to King's Island whenever you want aren't selling points for everyone. Listen, Gia, it could be worse. Your boyfriend might be 45th on the depth chart, but he still makes NFL money. You can fly to Miami. Some people are stuck in Ohio full time. Think of those poor souls! Brock Purdy is a fashion icon In an NFL where players arrive to the stadium decked out in designer outfits and carrying $20,000 Louis Vuitton bags (what are they even carrying in there?), you have to respect Brock Purdy's commitment to showing up every Sunday dressed like a Kohl's ad. Mr. Irrelevant. Forever humble. Apparently, Purdy's game-day fits have become enough of a thing that his wife, Jenna, showed him a post from a 49ers fan roasting his fashion choices. But this man is not trying to make a fashion statement. He just wants to be comfortable, darn it! And, honestly, Brock Purdy can show up to Levi's Stadium in cargo shorts, Crocs and a Kirkland Signature polo for all I care. The 49ers are 4-0, and through four weeks, he's playing as well as any quarterback in football. The NFL's own QB rankings have him at No. 1. Meanwhile, here in Tennessee, the Titans would settle for a quarterback who shows up dressed like the guy changing your oil at Jiffy Lube if he could win a football game. And at this point, Jiffy Lube guy might actually be an upgrade over Cam Ward. Not that I have any room to talk as a fan of the God-forsaken Miami Dolphins. Tankathon 2026, baby! Let's open the mailbag. 📩 Email: amber.harding@outkick.com (Send your thoughts, stories, tips, rants and photos of your dog.) 🐦 Twitter/X: @TheAmberHarding 📸 Instagram: @amberharding Last week, I had a dry inbox (very sad), but you all came through for today. I knew you would. Look at all these good boys and girls Gene in the Rock writes: Your empty mailbag... Positively NOT okay. I know you're up to your arse in largemoth bass with launching OKO, but I think I know what would fill it up. How about a Muttkick Outdoors column? Rocky would love you and so would we. Amber: You know, a weekly column all about dogs is not the worst idea I've ever heard. Let's start with this Corgi named Banana and his ice-cold look back. Eric P. writes: What do ya mean you have an empty mail box.. I look forward to see my friends every week.. -Duke Dusty T. writes: Here is a pic of our family hounds, Monroe (left) and Ladybug. This is what happens when it dips below 80 degrees in Phoenix... I know you were a writer for the Diamondbacks early in your career, so wanted to get your take on Torey Lovullo. Should they keep him? Amber: I like Torey Lovullo. The players seem to like playing for him, and I don't think all of the their recent shortcomings can fairly be pinned on the manager — especially with the injuries they've dealt with and the lack of consistent production at spots like first base and DH. He is the winningest manager in franchise history, after all, and got them to a World Series. At the same time, after 10 years, I understand the fanbase getting antsy. But it doesn’t matter what me or you or the man in the moon thinks because the D-backs already extended him for two more years. Jon C. writes: Hope your training [for the Spartan Race] pays off, as one of their tag lines says "You’ll know at the finish line". Looks like you’ll have the possibility of rain so more mud more fun. A few gear tips: 1 - everything dry fit. Don’t need anything that soaks up water because it will just weigh you down. 2 - knee high socks to cut down scrapes and scratches that you will collect. 3 - trail running shoes, more stable. Definite no on your typical waffle bottom jogging shoes. No grip and mud will collect and stick making feel like you are running with ankle weights. I initially looked at the Nashville race but then the football schedule came out and Vols home game so making the wife happy. Here is a dog pick from last summer at the UT Gardens on campus. SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER Amber: Don't be disappointed in me, Jon, but I decided not to do the Spartan Race this time around. First, the friend who was going to do it with me backed out. Then, I ended up having to travel a bunch over the past month, which would have severely derailed my training schedule. Excuses are like a**holes, everyone has one. I know. Or maybe that's what they say about opinions? Regardless, after middle Tennessee turned into a rainy, muddy mess on what would have been my race day this past Saturday, I'm kind of glad I bailed. And, hey, at least I didn't do this: Nebraska Niemo writes: So glad you got to spend some time on the water in Branson. Pretty nice place…not as nice as Pigeon Forge, you’re right…but pretty nice for the middle of America (approximately….I’m not a geographer). Just wanted your e-mail inbox to not be ‘empty’ this time. I want to do that with German Shepherds. I already have a sable — now I just need a white one, a black one, and a black and tan one. But first, I'd have to buy a bigger house, a bigger car and several more vacuum cleaners. articles.title: California couple with 21 children, most born via surrogates, charged in ‘house of horrors’ abuse case
articles.summary: A Southern California couple who had 21 children, most of whom were birthed by different surrogate mothers, lied to the surrogates and then subjected the children to vicious beatings and punishments, authorities said.
articles.body: A Southern California couple who had 21 children, most of whom were birthed by different surrogate mothers, lied to the surrogates and then subjected the children to vicious beatings and punishments, authorities said. Silvia Zhang and Guojun Xuan were arrested Tuesday after authorities served a search warrant at their Arcadia mansion as part of a child abuse investigation. They have been charged with conspiracy to commit child abuse and witness intimidation. Xuan also faces one felony count of child abuse, one felony count of accessory after the fact, and five felony counts of dissuading a witness. Zhang also faces one count of accessory after the fact and four counts of dissuading a witness. “This house could only be described as a house of horrors for these incredibly young children,” Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman said at a Tuesday news conference. Authorities began investigating the couple last year after a 2-month-old child was brought to the hospital with head injuries. Hochman, citing a criminal complaint, alleged that a nanny struck the baby in the head on May 4, 2025. Xuan and Zhang did not seek medical attention until days later, he said, noting that the baby has since recovered. During the investigation, authorities learned that Xuan and Zhang were running a surrogacy ring out of their home and hired surrogates throughout the country. Hochman said the couple often lied to the women about why they wanted children or how many children they already had. “One surrogate in particular … was paid for both a first and second surrogacy,” he said. “She was told initially Zhang was a single mother struggling to conceive when she agreed to act as a surrogate. That was a false statement.” The woman was paid up to $75,000 per surrogacy, the district attorney said. The couple failed to tell another woman who was 7 months pregnant that they already had 16 other children, he said. “Another surrogate, they said they were seeking the miracle baby, and they paid that surrogate $135,000,” Hochman said. Over the years, the children were allegedly abused while Xuan and Zhang watched on 32 motion-activated cameras they set up around the home, Hochman said. He described three rooms the couple called “learning rooms,” where the children would spend hours seated at desks under the supervision of various nannies. “Each one of these defendants monitored the nannies’ discipline of the children that were happening in the three learning centers,” the district attorney said. He said during one incident, a nanny had forced a child “to maintain a horse stance” and Xuan could be seen on video laughing. “In another situation, defendant Xuan entered one of the learning centers while a nanny was striking a child, and instructed the nanny to strike the child harder,” he said. Hochman alleged that Xuan also beat a child across the child’s bare buttocks and struck the child’s head. “Defendant Xuan also lifted the child into the air by one arm, while continuing to strike him and repeatedly struck the child’s head from side to side with sufficient force that the child’s body lurched into alternating directions with the blows,” he told reporters. He said the children were punished, physically abused and beaten “on a daily basis.” One room in the home did not have cameras. Hochman said the children would be taken into the room and could be heard “screaming from inside.” The couple is accused of trying to cover up the alleged abuse by instructing the children to lie, according to Hochman. During a meeting after the 2-month-old was taken to the hospital, the couple allegedly told the nannies not to leave visible marks on the children. “This case is unprecedented,” Hochman said. “It is horrific, and the physical abuse, beating, and punishment that these very young children received is despicable.” Los Angeles County Sheriff Robert G. Luna said the children were subjected to “horrific abuse.” Fifteen children were removed from the home last year, and another six were found to be in the care of family and friends. Xuan and Zhang are expected to be arraigned Tuesday. Prosecutors are seeking $100 million bail. An arrest warrant was previously issued for one of the nannies seen on video violently shaking the 2-month-old baby. The nanny has not been arrested.

articles.title: CBI raids CM Bhagwant Mann’s camp office, his OSD’s home in graft probe
articles.summary: NEW DELHI/CHANDIGARH: CBI registered an FIR against Punjab chief minister Bhagwant Mann’s OSD Rajbir Ghuman and five others Tuesday, following it up with
articles.body: NEW DELHI/CHANDIGARH: CBI registered an FIR against Punjab chief minister Bhagwant Mann’s OSD Rajbir Ghuman and five others Tuesday, following it up with raids on eight locations, including the CM’s camp office in Chandigarh.The coordinated search came within hours of the state govt moving Supreme Court against Punjab and Haryana high court’s order for a CBI probe into ED’s allegation that a bribe syndicate influenced transfers, postings, tenders and policy decisions through the OSD.The search at Mann’s camp office in House No 50 of Sector 2 started around 6pm, sending shockwaves through the administration. It was at this office that Ghuman used to allegedly meet the co-accused, said CBI sources. A CBI team also visited Ghuman’s home in his village, Gharachon in Sangrur.CBI said the case was registered following a court order that was based on an ED report. The investigation centres on allegations of corruption and abuse of power and political influence. Apart from Ghuman, those named by CBI in the FIR are Nitin Gohal, Jitin Gohal alias Raja, Romi Raja Mahajan, Bir Devinder, RS Nagra and “unknown public servant(s) and private person(s)”.Nitin is alleged to be a “liaison” in the “cash-for-transfer” scandal with access to Ghuman. His brother Jitin was allegedly provided access to CMO through Ghuman and Dr Romi Mahajan, described as an “associate” who allegedly worked with Ghuman and helped coordinate appointments. Devinder is an AAP youth activist and Nagra is a “private associate”.CBI searched premises linked to the accused in Chandigarh, Mohali, Gurdaspur, Ludhiana, Patiala, Sangrur and Jalandhar and seized laptops, mobile phones and financial documents.After CBI raid in graft probe, Punjab CM claims BJP has started poll preparationThe seized laptops, mobile phones and documents are currently undergoing forensic scrutiny to establish evidence of bribery, official impropriety, and financial paper trails.Punjab CM Bhagwant Mann responded through a post on X in Punjabi, “BJP has started preparations for Punjab elections. A CBI raid was conducted at my camp office. Now ED and CBI will be misused in Punjab so that Punjab govt and I can be defamed. BJP is in panic as it sees the love received from people.”CBI said the FIR is meant to investigate allegations of corruption against OSD to CM, Rajbir Ghuman, and his associates for “influencing and manipulating postings of officers, including that of IAS and IPS officers, departmental proceedings, matters pertaining to policy formulation, administrative approvals, tender conditions, licensing matters, land use conversion matters, property disputes, revenue and land-related issues in lieu of pecuniary benefits”.“It is also alleged that the accused public servants purportedly accessed and provided drafts of orders and policies to private persons prior to their issuance by the govt,” said CBI, adding that those named in the FIR include two public servants, middlemen, and associates.ED had conducted searches in Punjab from May 7-10 in a PMLA case and written to the DGP on July 30 to register a case.Advocate Nikhil Saraf filed a PIL in HC, alleging ED had written three letters to the Punjab DGP, seeking registration of an FIR against Ghuman and others, yet Punjab Police didn’t do so.On Monday, a division bench of Chief Justice Ashwani Kumar Mishra and Justice Rohit Kapoor heard the PIL and said, “We are not impressed by the manner in which Punjab Police has acted so far and, therefore, deem it appropriate to entrust investigation to CBI.”Get the latest India News and Live updates.
