articles.summary: She’s Alive, the entity that manages and protects Parton’s professional property, is suing Bryan Seaver, accusing him of threatening the late music icon’s legacy.
articles.body: Barbed wire, yellow caution tape and “no trespassing” signs. Attorneys for the estate of Dolly Parton claim that Bryan Seaver, the late country music icon’s nephew, used these items to barricade his property in an attempt to avoid being served with a lawsuit accusing him of threatening to destroy Parton’s legacy. The revelation came to light on Monday in court filings in which lawyers for the estate included images showing a “no trespassing” sign in Seaver’s front yard, and barbed wire and yellow caution tape wrapping the handrails leading to his front door. The photos were part of a court filing urging the judge overseeing the case to deny Seaver’s request for additional time to retain an attorney ahead of a temporary injunction hearing set for Friday. The legal ordeal between Seaver and She’s Alive, the entity in charge of managing and protecting Parton’s professional property and business, began two weeks ago, when the estate filed a civil complaint against the nephew. Seaver is the person the late star had handpicked to announce her death from cancer. She’s Alive, which is led by Parton’s longtime manager Danny Nozell, accused Seaver of waging a successful “campaign of threats” against its employees and business partners — causing many of them to quit their jobs, according to the complaint. The complaint included text messages and emails from Seaver. In one message he threatens to “set up a podcast dedicated to ruining Dolly’s brand partnerships and telling the violations these people have done on us. It’s going to be great. Or f------ pay me.” She’s Alive also claimed it was forced to hire private security for its remaining personnel, including at their homes, as a result of the threats. Court records state Seaver used to work for private military contractors before providing security services for Parton and her properties through his company, Squadron Augmented Protection Services. Court records still do not list an attorney for Seaver. On Tuesday, he did not respond to an email seeking comment. Seaver said in a recent text to The New York Times that his messages were twisted, writing, “This is a contrived out-of-context explanation of how this went down and it is being done in an effort to solidify me as some sort of opposition to her brand in her legacy.” She’s Alive removed Seaver from his security role about a week before filing its lawsuit, saying his “terrorizing conduct made their continued retention untenable.” Seaver was eventually served via email after She’s Alive unsuccessfully “tried to serve the summons, Verified Complaint, and injunction paper on Mr. Seaver on three occasions,” according to court records. Chancellor I’Ashea L. Myles, the judge overseeing the case, granted a temporary restraining order on Sept. 22 after reviewing text messages from Seaver that directed harmful threats “toward identifiable existing business relationships rather than merely expressing generalized dissatisfaction,” according to her ruling. Seaver also boasted about “his access to weapons, experience with violence, and intention to retaliate against persons whom he perceived to have acted against his family,” the ruling stated. The temporary restraining order intends to stop Seaver from talking with or being within 1,000 feet of any She’s Alive employees, attorneys and business partners. It is also meant to keep him from interfering with estate’s business relationships. The legal battle has gained national attention over the past few weeks after it offered initial signs of discord in a carefully managed estate process for one of the nation’s most beloved artists. Parton, who died Aug. 25, was a country music giant, philanthropist and cultural icon. She distinguished herself by writing hundreds of songs — including timeless hits like “Jolene,” “Coat of Many Colors” and “I Will Always Love You,” which earned over 100 million worldwide sales and more than 1 billion online streams.

articles.title: Newsom signs first-in-nation law forcing major companies to reveal slavery-era ties: 'Make it public'
articles.summary: California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed a first-in-the-nation law requiring large companies to disclose slavery-era transactions dating back to 1849.
articles.body: California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed a first-in-the-nation law Wednesday requiring large companies doing business in the state to scour historical records and publicly disclose slavery-era transactions, advancing California's broader reparations effort through a new corporate "accountability" mandate. Newsom’s office referred Fox News Digital to an Oct. 1 interview with civil rights attorney Bryan Stevenson, in which the governor signed the bill on camera and framed the measure as an effort to establish accountability through public disclosure. "This is a bill that requires large companies that operated before 1965 to search their records for ties to slavery going back to 1849 and then we make it public. These are insurance policies on enslaved people. Human beings used as collateral, quite literally as collateral for loans. Accountability, as Bryan said, starts with the truth," Newsom said. CALIFORNIA COUNTY APPROVES REPARATIONS PLAN AS NEIGHBORING SCHOOL DISTRICT 'BLACK THRIVING' EFFORT STALLS Assembly Bill 2599, authored by Democratic Assemblymember Isaac Bryan, applies to businesses with more than $100 million in annual worldwide gross receipts that existed, or have a predecessor company that existed, on or before Dec. 31, 1964. Once funded by the Legislature, covered companies must submit affidavits under penalty of perjury verifying searches for records involving the purchase or sale of enslaved people, their use as loan collateral, slave-related insurance and other transactions. The law also calls for the records to become publicly accessible through a state digital platform. For companies doing business in California as of Jan. 1, 2028, the first affidavits are due by Jan. 15, 2029, or later if the state's platform has not yet been developed. Bryan framed the measure as an effort to expose corporate wealth tied to slavery while presenting the bill before lawmakers in June. "For centuries, private corporations across the country benefited from chattel slavery," Bryan said during a Senate Standing Committee on Public Safety hearing. "They benefited from the economic wealth transfer of free labor." TRUMP ADMIN WANTS TO STOP ILLINOIS CITY'S REPARATIONS EFFORT FOR 'SIMPLY HANDING OUT MONEY BASED ON RACE' Fox News Digital reached out to Bryan for comment but did not immediately receive a response. The law came three years after California's first-in-the-nation Reparations Task Force issued more than 100 recommendations for addressing the effects of slavery and discrimination. The task force examined potential monetary compensation alongside policy changes involving housing, education, policing, health and economic disparities. Newsom previously stopped short of endorsing the task force’s proposed direct cash payments. In a 2023 statement to Fox News Digital, the governor said addressing slavery’s legacy extended beyond sending checks to eligible residents. "Dealing with that legacy is about much more than cash payments," Newsom said at the time. CASH PAYMENTS ARE NOT 'RULED OUT' AS CALIFORNIA COUNTY OFFICIALS PUSH REPARATIONS FOR BLACK LOCALS The task force's report cited JPMorgan Chase as one historical example, noting the banking giant apologized in 2005 after research found two predecessor banks had accepted approximately 13,000 enslaved people as collateral for loans and eventually took ownership of about 1,250 people when borrowers defaulted. The legislation faced opposition from several insurance industry groups, including the American Council of Life Insurers and American Property Casualty Insurance Association. California has required insurers to research and disclose slavery-era insurance policies since 2000, and the state maintains those records through its Department of Insurance. The California Senate Judiciary Committee’s analysis of the bill said five insurance industry groups opposed the bill, including the American Council of Life Insurers, the Association of California Life and Health Insurance Companies and the American Property Casualty Insurance Association. The committee analysis summarized their opposition as focused on potential duplication of slavery-era disclosures insurers were already required to make under a 2000 law. articles.title: Loyalty be damned: Did these coaches stick around a season too long and blow their chances at a big gig?
articles.summary: Kenny Dillingham, Jedd Fisch, and Brent Key were among college football's hottest coaching names. Now all three programs are struggling in 2025.
articles.body: I want to take you all back to January 2025. The Arizona State Sun Devils just completed an improbable run to the College Football Playoff only two years removed from the disastrous Herm Edwards era. Head coach Kenny Dillingham, in only his second year on the job, had guided the program through NCAA sanctions and three-win seasons to a Big 12 championship and had his team on the precipice of a Playoff win over Texas thanks to the contributions of exciting players like Cam Skattebo, Jordyn Tyson, and Sam Leavitt. SLEEPER TEAMS FROM EACH POWER 4 CONFERENCE: WHO WILL EXCEED EXPECTATIONS THIS COLLEGE FOOTBALL SEASON? Just two years later and the Sun Devils now sit at 2-2 with an anemic offense, fresh off a beatdown at the hands of Baylor, a team currently employing a coach who was on a ridiculously hot seat himself just a month earlier. Less than a year after Arizona State's magical CFP appearance, two more coaches were making names for themselves at schools on opposite ends of the country. Jedd Fisch inherited a Washington program in 2024 that had just competed for a national championship the season prior to his arrival, but had to replace almost 100% of the team's production from a year earlier. After a 6-7 campaign that year showed promise, Fisch followed that up with a nine-win season that included a bowl win over Boise State and featured a quarterback by the name of Demond Williams who was the toast of college football. LINCOLN RILEY HOT SEAT RUMORS GET LOUDER AFTER 'FIRE LINCOLN' CHANTS DURING USC-WASHINGTON Meanwhile, more than 2,600 miles to the southeast, Brent Key was turning Georgia Tech into a legitimate threat in the ACC with a super innovative offense and a Heisman hopeful by the name of Haynes King at quarterback. The Yellow Jackets climbed to as high as number seven in the AP Poll, their highest mark in nearly two decades, and even finished the season ranked for the first time since 2014. Ten months later, and both Washington and Georgia Tech - along with the aforementioned Sun Devils - look like shells of their former selves from just a season ago. It happens. These schools are not built to contend for more than a season or two in a row without sharp fluctuations year-to-year. THERE'S A DIFFERENCE BETWEEN COACHES WHO 'CAN'T' WIN A NATIONAL CHAMPIONSHIP AND COACHES WHO 'HAVEN'T' While programs like Ohio State, Texas, Oregon, and Georgia have the infrastructure, funding, and talent pipelines to be consistently great year in and year out, the Washingtons, Georgia Techs, and Arizona States of the world need to capitalize on razor thin windows and go "all in" whenever they recognize those windows are approaching. That goes for their coaches, too. There was a time when Dillingham, Fisch, and Key were being linked to every major job in college football following their respective "window years." Dillingham was talked about as Mike Norvell's potential replacement at Florida State following their abysmal 2024 season, and the 36-year-old head coach was even discussed for the Michigan job shortly after they fired Sherrone Moore. WHICH HEAD COACH'S SEAT IS HOTTER HEADING INTO 2026 SEASON: SHANE BEAMER OR MIKE NORVELL? Speaking of the Maize and Blue, Fisch was also thought to be the leader in the clubhouse to take the job in Ann Arbor, and both he and Key were heavily considered as candidates for the opening at Florida, with Fisch getting extra attention given his alumni status in Gainesville. These three coaches were some of the hottest names in the last two hiring cycles, and for whatever reason, they chose to stay at their respective spots. There's no shame in that, and for Dillingham and Key, it could also come down to the fact that they are coaching at their alma maters. But the question remains: did they miss their chance to parlay their successful seasons into jobs at bigger, more established programs? If Washington, Arizona State, and Georgia Tech all finish with six or seven losses each this season, their respective coaches likely won't be fielding many calls when high-level jobs come open in November. Perhaps they're happy where they are now, although Dillingham has specifically called out Arizona State's fanbase and booster clubs about a lack of funding in the past, and based on conversations I've had with people close to the Gators' football program regarding the Florida job, it's one that Fisch would readily take under the right circumstances. Time will tell for all three of these coaches, as well as others who are making a name for themselves at the "mid-tier" Power 4 programs. COLLEGE FOOTBALL WEEK 4 CONTENDERS, PRETENDERS: TEXAS SURVIVES, MICHIGAN'S KARMA AND COACHES ARE SWEATING Maybe one of these three will win 10 or 11 games in 2027 and land a tier-one job to make me look like a fool. It worked for Matt Campbell, who had multiple historic seasons at Iowa State in 2020 and 2024 only to turn down other offers. It was only after Penn State came calling a year later that Campbell finally decided to leave the comfort of Ames. Patience is a virtue, as is loyalty, but when it comes to being a college football coach, sometimes those things can come back to bite you in the rear end. You're only as good as your latest season, and a lot of these hiring athletic directors have a bad case of recency bias when it comes to selecting their next football coach. I'll be interested to see where Kenny Dillingham, Brent Key, and Jedd Fisch are a year from today. Will they be settling in at cushy new jobs in Tallahassee, Los Angeles, and Norman? Or will they be the latest victims of the "what have you done for me lately" league that is Power 4 college football? CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP There's only one way to find out.

articles.title: US death row inmate Christa Pike conscious after failed execution, lawyers say
articles.summary: Pike, 50, continues to receive critical medical care while handcuffed in hospital, according to a statement from her lawyers on Tuesday.
articles.body:
US death row inmate Christa Pike is "conscious and speaking" after her failed execution attempt, her lawyers say.

Pike, 50, continues to receive critical medical care while handcuffed in hospital, according to a statement from her attorneys on Tuesday.

She was sentenced to death following her conviction for murdering Colleen Slemmer in 1995. But Pike survived two lethal injections last week and was transferred to a hospital in Nashville, Tennessee, for treatment.

Her lawyers had said in the days afterwards that she was unconscious while medical staff cleared her body of the pentobarbitol injected during the failed execution attempt.

Pike's lawyers said on Tuesday that her recovery is "medically unprecedented", and while her prognosis remains unclear, "at a minimum, we expect a long recovery".

They said she is the only person known to have survived a completed execution attempt in the US.

Authorities have not yet said whether they will try again to execute Pike. They have also not offered an explanation for what went wrong.

Tennessee Governor Bill Lee suspended all executions for the rest of the year - and the head of prisons in the state said over the weekend that he plans to resign.

Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer, whom they had met at a job training camp for troubled teens.

articles.title: Christa Pike is awake and speaking after failed execution, lawyer says
articles.summary: The Tennessee woman who survived an execution last week is conscious, speaking and receiving medical care in a development her attorneys described Tuesday as “unprecedented.”
articles.body: The Tennessee woman who survived an execution last week is conscious, speaking and receiving medical care in a development her attorneys described Tuesday as “unprecedented.” In a statement, attorneys for Christa Pike said she remains handcuffed and shackled despite suffering significant injuries to her arms after two lethal injections of pentobarbital failed to kill her. The statement described her prognosis as unclear. “At a minimum, we expect a long recovery,” attorneys Randy Spivey and Kelly Gleason said. “We are incredibly grateful to the first responders and the medical team at the hospital who treated Christa like a human and have provided exceptional care to her. We also want to thank thousands from all over the world who sent messages offering prayers and support for Christa.” The statement said the attorneys will speak during a news conference Wednesday.
